sections.title: Foreword
sections.html:
There is a difference between knowing about God and knowing God. The first can be taught in a classroom, examined in a discussion and expressed in carefully chosen words. The second reaches beyond what a person can explain and begins to change how that person lives.

Both matter. We should seek to understand what we believe, but we must also recognise that an accurate account of God is not the whole of our need. We can become familiar with the language of faith while remaining strangers to the wonder it expresses.

Exploring the Godhead invites the reader into an enquiry whose purpose extends beyond understanding a doctrine to knowing the God of whom it speaks.

That is a considerable undertaking, especially with a subject many people approach with hesitation. Some assume it belongs chiefly to theologians; others have learned to repeat its familiar expressions without asking what they mean. Cheta Mbadinuju takes that hesitation seriously and gives the reader reason to continue.

He writes as a man who has wrestled honestly before writing confidently. That distinction is significant because readers can often sense when an author has passed too quickly over the very questions troubling them. Here, there is room to pause, consider and ask again.

His legal background lends the writing a habit of careful enquiry. He pays attention to words, examines the grounds of an assertion and understands that a conclusion should be supported. The reader is welcomed into that process in language that makes participation possible.

I particularly appreciate the respect this shows the ordinary reader. A person who brings an honest question deserves an answer that can be understood and considered.

Throughout this enquiry, Scripture remains the governing authority. The book’s confidence rests on attending patiently to what God has made known, rather than seeking novelty for its own sake. Its invitation is to look more carefully at truths whose familiarity may have concealed their significance.

What we need is for the truth God has revealed to become more clearly understood and more deeply received. The mind must be engaged, but the enquiry should also reach our trust, our worship and our daily conduct. A book serves us well when it encourages that fuller response without pretending it can produce it on our behalf.

I believe pastors will find material here that sharpens their teaching and renews their appreciation of its subject. Students of Scripture will find encouragement to examine familiar passages with greater care. Ordinary believers will find an invitation to think seriously about the God they confess.

Thoughtful readers will find a welcome in these pages, including those whose questions remain unresolved.

My hope is that you will give this book the attention its subject deserves. Allow its questions to settle, consider the Scriptures it presents and approach familiar truths with fresh attention. You may discover that what you thought you knew still has much to teach you.

I commend Exploring the Godhead with the prayer that its influence will continue beyond the final page. May it deepen your understanding, strengthen your faith and renew your desire to seek God.

Above all, may the God to whom these pages direct you become more clearly known and more deeply trusted in your own life.

Apostle Gordon Ada Gordon-Osagiede Jr
Spirit & Life Family Bible Church (SLFBC) Global
Abuja, FCT, Nigeria

sections.title: Preface
sections.html:
This book explores a conviction that is simple to state but far-reaching in its implications: the knowledge of God is the foundation on which every other form of understanding finally rests.

That does not mean theology can answer every question in science, medicine, law, economics or public life. Each field has its own methods, evidence and expertise, and knowing God does not remove the need for research, professional competence or sound judgment.

The claim reaches beneath those fields. We can discover how something works without knowing why it exists or what it is ultimately for. We can recognise a person’s worth without agreeing on where that worth comes from. We can acquire remarkable powers without gaining the wisdom to use them well.

The knowledge of God asks us to consider the larger reality within which human enquiry takes place.

The book therefore examines, through the Bible, the belief that knowing God gives us a foundation for understanding our past, our present lives and the future we face. It asks what follows if that claim is true: how might it change the way we understand ourselves, order our lives and take part in the world?

Christian faith is the starting point, but difficult questions are welcome and every conclusion is open to examination. Scripture provides the governing authority, while history, reason and hard objections test whether the Christian understanding has been expressed faithfully.

At the centre of the enquiry is the one living God whom Scripture reveals as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The infinite God cannot be contained within a human argument, and this book does not try to explain everything about Him. Its purpose is to consider what God has chosen to reveal and to follow the consequences of that revelation as far as these pages permit.

This is not a complete account of Christian theology, an exhaustive history of doctrine or an attempt to settle every controversy surrounding the Trinity. It is an exploration written for readers who may differ in background, experience and belief.

Some readers will recognise its language from a lifetime in the Church; others will have heard its claims without considering their bearing on ordinary life. Some may still be uncertain whether those claims are true.

Each reader is invited to examine the argument, weigh the objections and ask whether the God revealed in Scripture provides a foundation from which creation, human dignity, redemption, purpose and history become more fully understandable.

The title uses the word Godhead, a term found in the King James Version, while Trinity is used when referring more specifically to the historic Christian formulation. Neither word replaces the language of Scripture or reduces God to a formula. Both point towards the reality this book explores: the one God who has made Himself known as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

My work as a commercial lawyer and entrepreneur has shaped the way I approach the enquiry. Legal practice has taught me to pay attention to evidence, language and competing interpretations. Business has shown me how much distance there can be between an attractive idea and its consequences.

Those habits help me ask questions; they cannot settle the answers in advance. God is neither a problem to be solved nor an object over which human reason has final authority. The task is more modest: to listen to what God has disclosed, think honestly about its meaning and acknowledge where the subject exceeds our understanding.

The pages that follow are offered as an invitation: to know God more truly and, in knowing Him, to begin understanding everything else. They ask whether the God we may know about has become the God in whose light we see the world and whether truths we profess have begun to shape the lives we live.

The Prologue tells how that enquiry became personal, and why a commercial lawyer whose life appeared directed elsewhere found himself writing a book about the Godhead.

Unless otherwise indicated, Scripture quotations are from the King James Version, chosen for its familiar language and enduring influence, without diminishing the value of other faithful translations.

sections.title: Prologue
sections.subtitle: Between Two Callings
sections.html:
If you know me, this book will probably surprise you.

Most people encounter me first as a lawyer, more particularly, a business and finance lawyer. For much of my professional life, I have advised entrepreneurs, negotiated commercial transactions, structured investments and helped businesses work through legal and economic complexity.

My days have been occupied with contracts rather than creeds, boardrooms rather than Bible colleges, and commercial strategy rather than theological reflection. For that reason alone, few would have expected my first book to be about the Godhead.

Those familiar with me beyond my professional life might be even more surprised. They have seen my enthusiasm for business, leadership, economics, sports and public policy. Even among fellow Christians, it would have seemed far more natural for me to write about law, governance or enterprise than about the doctrine of the Trinity.

The obvious question follows: Why would a commercial lawyer write a book about God?

The answer does not begin with theology. It begins with an assumption that quietly shaped much of my adult life.

Although I was brought up by Christian parents and regarded my faith as the defining truth of my life, I never imagined that Christian writing would become part of my calling. I believed the Scriptures, loved the Church and sought to honour Christ within my profession whenever I could.

I simply assumed that the serious work of theological reflection belonged to others, while mine belonged to the marketplace.

That assumption seemed entirely reasonable because I grew up watching a man whose calling appeared unmistakably different.

My late father was trained in law, journalism and political science. He served his community, state and country in various appointed and elected capacities. None of those roles, however, became the defining pursuit of his life.

Following his conversion to Christ in 1983, every aspect of his public service, leadership, legal career, writing and ministry found its place beneath a greater allegiance. Whether practising law, serving in government, teaching the Scriptures, writing books or establishing a ministry and Foundation, he remained, before everything else, a disciple of Jesus Christ.

Only later did I appreciate the lesson his life had been teaching me all along.

Faith is not an addition to one’s vocation. It is the ground from which every vocation derives its meaning.

That was the environment in which I was raised. The Christian home my parents nurtured, the Scriptures my father taught and the books he wrote shaped my understanding of God long before I recognised their lasting influence.

Although my own path led me into business, finance and legal practice, those foundations never left me. Even so, I had unconsciously divided our lives into two distinct callings: his belonged to Christian ministry, public service and community development; mine belonged to commerce and the law.

For years, that distinction seemed perfectly natural.

It began to disappear on 11 April 2023, when my father departed to be with the Lord.

Like every son who loses his father, I grieved. There were responsibilities to shoulder, a family to support and a Foundation to help steward into its next chapter. I expected the months ahead to be consumed by practical demands.

Instead, they became a season of deep reflection.

As preparations began for my father’s State burial, I searched for a souvenir that could be shared with those who came to honour him. I wanted something more enduring than a conventional memorial brochure, something that would allow those who knew him in public life to encounter the faith that had sustained his private life.

That search led me back to the archives of his Christian literature, which I had helped curate for the Foundation.

I knew those books. I had handled them, preserved them and understood their place within his legacy. Bereavement made me read them differently.

I was no longer reading merely as his son or as curator of his literary work. I was reading the words of a man whose earthly life was complete, a man who had known public office and private adversity, achievement and disappointment, prominence and retirement, and had now passed beyond them all.

One book stood out.

In 1988, eleven years before he became Governor of Anambra State, my father had written God’s Kind of Leader: A Righteous and Responsible Man. I eventually chose it as the book to be distributed at the State burial.

The chronology struck me. These were convictions about God, leadership, righteousness and responsibility expressed long before political office came. They had preceded the challenges he later encountered and the achievements by which many people came to know him.

The book went beyond an account of leadership to reveal a conviction my father held deeply: that the true measure of a leader lies not in the authority he wields, but in the character with which he exercises it and his ultimate accountability to God.

That discovery sent me back to the wider body of Christian literature he had left behind. I was now reading to understand the vision of God and the life they expressed.

What had sustained such confidence through the changing circumstances of one man’s life? What was left when office, achievement and public recognition had become matters of history?

The questions began to turn from my father and the life he had lived towards me, asking what gave my own life its meaning and direction.

What would remain when my own professional achievements, business interests and public responsibilities had passed into memory? What had I treated as foundational simply because it was immediate, productive or visible? Had I inherited the convictions that shaped my father’s life, or merely become familiar with the language in which he expressed them?

At the same time, I witnessed the faithfulness of God extending beyond the life of the man who had consistently proclaimed Him. Responsibilities that had appeared overwhelming were met with unexpected grace. The family endured, the law practice evolved, the Foundation continued and new expressions of my father’s legacy began to emerge.

These developments did not take away the grief. They showed me that God had been faithful in the midst of it.

Gradually, one truth became impossible to ignore. The greatest inheritance my father left me was neither his books, his public service nor the legacy associated with his name. It was the knowledge of God that had shaped every one of those things.

The Christian upbringing I had perhaps taken for granted while pursuing a profession outside formal Christian ministry had become the lens through which I now understood grief, purpose, responsibility and hope. What I had long regarded as the background of my life revealed itself to be its foundation.

That realisation did not immediately persuade me to write a book. It persuaded me to begin an investigation.

The investigation did not begin by asking whether God exists, which had long been settled, or whether the Christian faith is true. It began with questions that were both wider and more personal.

In an age of scientific and technological achievement, does the knowledge of God still occupy the central place it ought to hold? Have we gained an extraordinary understanding of the world while gradually losing sight of its Creator?

Was the God whose faithfulness I had witnessed in my father’s life still governing mine amid law, business, filial and public duties? If He has revealed Himself in Scripture, what does it mean to know Him as the living God through whom everything else finds meaning?

Those questions made this enquiry unavoidable.

They also gave the exploration its central question: if the knowledge of God is the foundation for understanding our past, our present realities and our future hope, what follows for the way we live now?

The word exploring is deliberate. I do not approach the Godhead as a subject that can be mastered, nor do I presume at the beginning to know where every part of the enquiry will lead. The purpose is to follow the biblical witness as faithfully as possible, face the questions and objections that arise, and discover whether knowing God more truly can help us live with greater clarity and purpose.

Part I asks the question on which the rest of this book depends: why should the knowledge of God matter to the way we understand anything else? How can God be known and is knowing about Him the same as knowing Him?

Part II asks who the God we claim to know has revealed Himself to be. It examines what grounds the Christian confession of one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, whether the Church’s historic language faithfully expresses what Scripture reveals, and whether that confession can withstand the objections raised against it.

Part III asks what difference the Triune God makes beyond the words in which we confess Him. It follows His presence and activity in creation and providence, redemption and salvation, the believer’s life, and the worship and ministry of the Church.

Part IV asks what follows if knowing God is indeed foundational. It considers how that knowledge can help us come to terms with our past, live today, face the future and understand our responsibilities to one another, and what it might mean for human dignity, leadership and the civilisation we are helping to build.

The Epilogue returns to the personal story with which the book began. It leaves the enquiry open, reflecting on where it has led and why the odyssey into the light must continue beyond the final page.

The discipline of law and my Christian faith now meet within these pages. The first has trained me to question easy conclusions; the second reminds me that God is the living God who calls us to know Him, not a subject to be analysed.

For years, I thought those callings belonged to different parts of my life. I no longer do. This book stands at their meeting point. My father’s life brought me to the threshold of this enquiry. What he taught me cannot answer its questions on my behalf, and the reader need not share my history to ask them.

Our exploration therefore begins at the foundation: in a world that knows so much, why should the knowledge of God matter to how we understand the past, make sense of present realities and live with purpose as we look to the future with hope?

sections.title: Part I
sections.subtitle: The Question of the Godhead
sections.html:
“ …there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land.” Hosea 4:1

Who is God?

Hosea spoke to a people who knew the name of God and had heard His law. But he found a land in which truth, mercy and the knowledge of God were missing. Familiarity with His words had not ensured faithfulness to Him.

The distinction matters beyond Hosea’s time. We may speak confidently about God while giving little thought to who He is or how knowing Him should shape our lives. Before considering what that knowledge means for our identity, purpose and future, we must ask: Who is the God we claim to know?

Few questions have shaped human history as much. Civilisations have ordered their laws, customs and hopes around their answers. Philosophers have debated it, religions have offered their accounts, and people in every age have sought either to answer it or to live without settling it.

Even leaving the question unanswered has consequences. We still make decisions about what deserves our loyalty, what gives life meaning and whether we are accountable beyond ourselves. Our lives proceed upon convictions that we may never have examined.

Every enquiry requires clarity about its subject. In an enquiry into God, we must ask both whom we are seeking and how we could know Him.

Our enquiry begins with the world familiar to us. Humanity has extraordinary knowledge and increasing power, but can our discoveries settle the questions of purpose and responsibility, or do they bring those questions into sharper focus?

We must then ask how God could be known at all: what creation can tell us about Him, and what He must disclose for us to know Him more fully. We will also ask whether the early Church, in expressing its faith in creeds, introduced a new meaning or guarded the testimony it had received.

Finally, the enquiry comes closer to home. Can a person affirm what is true about God and still fail to know Him? What separates familiarity with Christian teaching from a life shaped by the God of whom it speaks?

People who do not acknowledge God can make real discoveries, recognise moral obligations and live generously. Christians, meanwhile, can confess their faith accurately while acting in ways that contradict it.

Neither observation should be explained away. Together, they require us to distinguish what people know, how they live and the foundation upon which their convictions rest.

The claim before us is substantial: that knowing God provides a foundation for understanding ourselves and everything else. It cannot be established simply by repeating it, nor should it be dismissed before its meaning and grounds have been examined.

Hosea’s warning stands. We may know the name, repeat the words and still have much to discover about the One of whom we speak.

Our enquiry begins with the question itself: Who is God?

sections.title: The Foundation of Everything Else
sections.html:
A World Rich in Knowledge

We know more about the world than any earlier generation. We can observe distant galaxies, examine the smallest structures of living organisms and communicate across continents almost instantly.

Medicine can detect conditions earlier generations scarcely understood. Technology has placed capabilities once confined to imagination within ordinary human reach.

Artificial intelligence now reads scans, drafts contracts and writes code. We have built systems that do more than store what we know; they increasingly influence how knowledge is organised, interpreted and used.

These achievements are real, and they show what human beings can discover and create within a world of remarkable order.

Scripture gives Christians no reason to deny them. Its opening chapters present human beings as made in God’s image and entrusted with work in His creation. Our capacity to observe, reason, build and organise belongs to that calling.

The Bible’s account of civilisation records the building of cities, the development of musical instruments and the working of brass and iron (Genesis 4:17–22). People can discover truths and contribute to human flourishing whether or not they consciously acknowledge God.

Humanity plainly knows a great deal without acknowledging God. What is in doubt is whether that knowledge can answer every question about the world and our place within it.

Understanding how the world works is a great achievement. An explanation of its processes, however, does not necessarily settle the questions of why it exists or what our lives within it mean.

A map remains useful even though it cannot decide where the traveller should go.

Capability Is Not Wisdom

Knowledge tells us what we can do. Wisdom asks whether an action is right, what purpose it serves and what it may cost others.

We have transformed many of the tools with which civilisation is built. New tools do not by themselves make us wiser or more compassionate. Ambition, greed, courage and the desire for recognition are as familiar as ever.

C. S. Lewis warned in The Abolition of Man (1943) that humanity’s growing control over nature might also give some people greater power over others. His concern was whether those who gained that power would have the moral judgment to use it well.

That concern is easy to recognise today. Artificial intelligence may improve diagnosis and expand education. It may also intensify surveillance, repeat prejudice or make it harder to identify who is responsible when a decision causes harm.

The ability to do something cannot, by itself, establish that it ought to be done. Capability needs direction, and those who exercise it are responsible for its consequences.

Scripture expresses the foundation of wisdom in these words:

“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.” Proverbs 9:10

The verse does not diminish learning or professional skill. It asks what should govern them. Biblical wisdom begins with the recognition that human beings did not create themselves and are not answerable only to themselves.

A sceptic might reasonably observe that people can think clearly, learn from experience, exercise sound moral judgment and lead meaningful lives without religious faith.

Questions We Cannot Avoid

Many who do not profess faith in God keep promises, care for families, oppose injustice and sacrifice for others. Denying their goodness would be inaccurate and unfair.

Human beings also do not need to resolve every question about God before recognising that children should be protected or cruelty opposed. Scripture itself speaks of those who, without possessing the written law, still show an awareness of moral obligation through conscience (Romans 2:14–15).

Believers do not always behave better than unbelievers, and a person need not first explain the source of morality before making a sound moral judgment.

The deeper question concerns the foundation of that judgment. If every human life has equal dignity, does that dignity depend on intelligence, usefulness or society’s willingness to recognise it? What gives justice its claim upon us when honouring it is costly?

The biblical answer begins with creation:

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.” Genesis 1:27

On this account, human worth is inherent, not conferred by status or achievement. It does not diminish when a person becomes ill, dependent, unproductive or powerless. Governments and institutions are bound to respect that worth; it is not theirs to grant or revoke.

A sceptic will ask why the biblical account should be accepted when religions offer different accounts of reality. Chapter Two takes up the question of authority, and Chapter Six the objections.

None of this is established yet. But our convictions about power, human worth and accountability already shape ordinary life, and we live by our answers to them.

What Do We Mean by Understanding?

We may understand how something works without knowing what place it should have in our lives.

We can describe the processes associated with death, but that description does not tell us how mortality should shape our choices. We can calculate the commercial value of almost anything, but calculation cannot tell us whether everything of value should be sold.

The distinction is familiar in legal practice. An agreement may meet formal requirements and still take advantage of a weaker party. Knowing how to make it enforceable does not settle whether we ought to enter into it.

The prophet Jeremiah addressed people familiar with the attraction of wisdom, power and wealth:

“Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me.” Jeremiah 9:23–24

The passage does not declare learning, strength or wealth worthless; it challenges the confidence we place in them. However much we possess, we must still ask whether we understand what our lives are for.

In his Confessions (Book I), Augustine described the human heart as restless until it finds rest in God. Achievement may fulfil our ambitions without satisfying our deepest longing.

John Calvin likewise observed, at the opening of the Institutes, that knowledge of God and knowledge of ourselves are deeply connected. It brings the enquiry closer to home: can we fully understand who we are while leaving aside the One from whom, according to Scripture, our lives proceed?

The Christian claim goes beyond adding God to the subjects we study. Knowing Him changes how we understand our place in the world and the responsibilities that come with it.

If creation belongs to God, our use of it must honour our responsibility to its Creator. If human beings bear His image, their worth limits what we may do to them, even when profit, convenience or the law permits it.

And if life is received from God, its purpose must be sought in relation to Him. Understanding ourselves would then involve more than discovering our abilities or deciding what we want.

These conclusions depend on whether the God of whom Scripture speaks is real and whether He has made Himself known. Both must be examined.

The Foundation Beneath the Questions

A foundation is rarely the most visible part of a structure. We notice its design, its height and the life taking place within it. The soundness of what we see, however, depends on what lies beneath.

Our decisions also rest on foundations we may seldom examine. We hold convictions about what is true, what people deserve and what makes a life worth living. Those convictions influence our choices even when we have never clearly put them into words.

A. W. Tozer began The Knowledge of the Holy by arguing that what we think of God is the most important thing about us. Our understanding of Him can shape what we trust, what we fear and what we believe is required of us.

A person who believes God is indifferent may see little reason to seek His guidance. Another who assumes that God approves whatever he desires may never pause to question whether his desires accord with God's will. Belief, then, is not beyond examination. What we believe about God matters profoundly, for our understanding of who He is inevitably shapes how we relate to Him and how we live.

If God is indeed our Creator, the Source of our existence and the One to whom we are ultimately accountable, then knowing Him cannot be confined to religious observance or private conviction. It reaches into every dimension of life: our work and relationships, our ambitions and responsibilities, the choices we make in public and the decisions we face when no one is watching.

Yet knowing God does not remove life's uncertainties, spare believers from suffering or make them immune to error. Faith does not promise a life without difficulty. The deeper question is whether knowing God provides a foundation upon which to face these realities, a perspective through which to understand them and a direction by which to navigate them.

That is the proposition at the heart of this book.

Human achievement gives us no reason to set the enquiry aside. The more power we acquire over the world and one another, the more consequential our convictions become.

But an enquiry into God faces a difficulty from the outset. How can human beings know the One whom Scripture presents as the source of their existence? What can creation tell us about Him, and what must we depend on Him to disclose?

Before we ask what it means to know God, we must ask how He makes Himself known.

sections.title: Revelation, Confession and the Creeds
sections.html:
The Question of Authority

One of the earliest lessons I learnt in legal practice was that confidence does not establish a case. Witnesses may disagree, experts may reach different conclusions and advocates may speak with equal conviction. A sound judgment requires us to examine the authority upon which each claim rests and whether the evidence can bear the weight placed upon it.

The search for knowledge of God presents a question of authority with consequences greater than those of any legal dispute. Who is competent to speak for Him? Can we come to know God through reason, religious instinct or scientific enquiry alone? Or must that knowledge ultimately come from God Himself?

The Christian answer begins with an assertion: we know God because He has chosen to make Himself known. Our task is to examine that claim and understand the testimony upon which it rests.

In the biblical account, God’s initiative stands at the beginning of our knowledge of Him. Before there was a prophet to proclaim Him, a theologian to describe Him or a creed to confess Him, there was the God who spoke.

Scripture reveals God as Creator, who calls the world into being, makes Himself known to Abraham and Moses, establishes His covenant with Israel and speaks through the prophets. This unfolding revelation finds its fulfilment in His Son.

At each stage, people respond to an initiative they did not originate. They may question, resist, misunderstand or obey, but what is made known to them begins with God.

Moses expressed both the privilege and the limit of that disclosure:

“The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever…” Deuteronomy 29:29

The distinction gives us two responsibilities. We must recognise the limits of what God has disclosed, and we must attend to what He has made known.

It takes humility to accept that some questions will go unanswered, and responsibility to refuse to use them as an excuse for neglecting the answers we have received.

Paul addresses the limits of human wisdom when he writes:

“…the world by wisdom knew not God…” 1 Corinthians 1:21

Paul is not dismissing intelligence or learning. In the surrounding passage, he confronts the expectation that God’s saving action must conform to human judgments about what is wise or impressive. The proclamation of Christ crucified challenges those expectations.

We can investigate creation skilfully, but knowing its Creator requires more than observing His works. We must ask whether He has spoken and how we can recognise His voice.

The Epistle to the Hebrews places this claim at its opening:

“God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,

Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son…” Hebrews 1:1–2

Here is the basis upon which Christian knowledge of God proceeds: He has spoken through the prophets and, decisively, in His Son. Christian theology must therefore attend to what He has said, rather than require Him to conform to the God we would prefer.

What Creation Can and Cannot Tell Us

God’s revelation does not make reason, conscience or the created order irrelevant. Within the Christian account, these are among the means through which His witness reaches us.

Reason enables us to investigate nature, distinguish sound arguments from careless ones and examine the claims presented to us. We depend on it when reading Scripture as surely as when studying the world around us.

Creation itself bears testimony. Paul writes:

“…the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made…” Romans 1:20

According to Paul, the things God has made disclose something of their Maker. Their testimony concerns His eternal power and Godhead. Creation does not tell us everything about Him, but neither does it leave us without a witness.

Its order, beauty and intelligibility raise questions about its source. We may investigate its processes while still asking why there is a world with such processes to investigate.

Conscience brings the enquiry into human experience. Paul describes people who do not possess the written law, yet:

“…shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness…” Romans 2:15

We disagree about particular moral judgments, and conscience can be mistaken or resisted. Still, the experience of obligation is familiar. We recognise that some things ought to be done even when they are inconvenient, and that some things are wrong even when they benefit us.

Christian theology commonly describes what God makes known through creation and conscience as general revelation. It is accessible to humanity at large, including those who do not possess the Scriptures.

What God makes known, however, is not always willingly received. Paul’s account in Romans addresses both the knowledge available to humanity and our resistance to it.

This is a difficulty we can recognise in ourselves. We readily accept evidence that supports our wishes and examine unwelcome evidence more severely. Where God is concerned, we may likewise prefer an account of Him that leaves our ambitions undisturbed.

There are also limits to what creation and conscience disclose. Neither tells us, by itself, that the eternal Word became flesh, that Christ died for sinners or that the Holy Spirit dwells within those who belong to Him.

Conscience may make us aware of guilt. It cannot, on its own authority, announce God’s provision for forgiveness.

These truths depend on a more particular disclosure: God’s words and saving acts, recorded in Holy Scripture and brought to their fulfilment in Jesus Christ. Christian theology commonly describes this as special revelation.

The distinction concerns both the means and the content of what is revealed. Creation bears witness to its Maker; Scripture makes known His saving purposes and the acts through which He fulfils them.

Reason is active throughout. We must assess claims to revelation, interpret what we read, test its coherence and distinguish faithful understanding from distortion. Calling something revelation does not exempt its claim from examination.

Once received as God’s revelation, however, it must be allowed to challenge our assumptions. We cannot reasonably seek knowledge of Him while deciding beforehand that He may disclose only what we already find acceptable.

The doctrine of the Godhead therefore begins with the testimony Scripture gives. We must examine what it says about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, allowing the whole account to shape our understanding of God.

When Revelation Required Confession

Revelation brings a further responsibility. If God has made Himself known, how should His people express what they have received?

The obvious answer is to use the words of Scripture. Those words must remain central, but quoting them does not automatically settle their meaning. Two people can repeat the same passage while making very different claims.

Every reader brings assumptions to a text. Our ideas about God, language, personhood and what we consider possible can influence what we notice and what we overlook. Careful interpretation requires us to recognise those influences rather than imagine that we have none.

The difficulty becomes serious when biblical language is retained while the meaning attached to it changes. Agreement in wording can conceal disagreement about the very matter being confessed.

The early Church faced this problem in its teaching about God. Scripture affirmed that there is one God. It also spoke of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in ways that required the Church to take their deity seriously, while preserving the distinctions between them.

The responsibility was to account for these claims together. A proposed explanation could clarify one passage while making another difficult to acknowledge.

Some teachings defended divine unity by treating the Son as a created being. Others spoke of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit as different manifestations of one person, removing the real distinctions Scripture presents.

These explanations offered an apparent simplicity. Each, however, achieved that simplicity by surrendering part of the testimony it was meant to explain.

The difficulty is familiar in legal argument. One real fact may support a plausible account until other material facts are considered. A sound judgment must address the evidence that challenges a theory as fully as the evidence that favours it.

The same discipline matters here. An account of God must do justice to Scripture’s affirmation of His unity, its testimony concerning the deity of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and its distinction between them.

The Church could not resolve the matter merely by selecting whichever claim seemed easiest to explain. Its confession had to preserve the testimony as a whole, including truths whose relation it could affirm without fully comprehending.

This was the responsibility within which the creeds took shape. They gave the Church a means of stating what it understood Scripture to teach and of identifying interpretations that departed from that understanding.

The question to ask of these formulations is plain: did they preserve the meaning of the biblical testimony, or introduce claims that the testimony could not sustain? To answer it, we must examine both the language the Church adopted and the errors it sought to exclude.

The Creeds Take Shape

Long before the great councils, Christians confessed their faith in concise forms. The Church baptised in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Believers summarised the Gospel they had received and distinguished apostolic teaching from counterfeits.

Confession belonged to the life of the Church before it became the language of controversy.

The Apostles’ Creed emerged from this early confessional and baptismal tradition. It was not written by the Apostles themselves, despite the name by which it became known. Its significance lies in the way it gathers the central affirmations of the apostolic faith into a brief and memorable form.

Its structure is unmistakably Trinitarian. It confesses God the Father Almighty, Jesus Christ His only Son, and the Holy Ghost. It moves through creation, incarnation, suffering, resurrection, judgment, the Church, forgiveness and everlasting life.

As new disputes arose, however, greater precision became necessary.

In the early fourth century, Arius taught in a manner that sought to preserve the supreme uniqueness of the Father by denying the full and eternal deity of the Son. The Son could be exalted above all other creatures, but He remained on the created side of the divide.

The attraction of the position should not be caricatured. Arius was attempting to defend monotheism and account for biblical passages that speak of the Son in relation to the Father.

The proposal nevertheless failed to preserve the whole biblical witness. If the Son is not truly God, then the One through whom Christians believed they had encountered God does not fully reveal Him. The One they worship is not entitled to that worship, and the salvation attributed to Him is placed upon the shoulders of a creature.

The Council of Nicaea in A.D. 325 answered by confessing the Son as “of one substance” with the Father. The term was not intended to introduce a second authority beside Scripture. It closed an interpretative escape route through which biblical expressions could be repeated while the Son was still treated as less than God.

The Church was stating what it understood those expressions necessarily to mean: the Son shares fully in the one divine being.

Controversy continued after Nicaea, and the confession was developed at Constantinople in A.D. 381. The creed associated with Nicaea and Constantinople affirms the full deity of the Son and expresses more fully the Church’s confession of the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, and Giver of life.”

The Church sharpened its language because the errors it faced had sharpened, not because God had changed.

The Athanasian Creed belongs to a later Western tradition. It was not written by Athanasius, though it reflects the doctrinal cause he defended with extraordinary courage.

Its more elaborate language insists that Christians must neither confuse the Persons nor divide the divine being. The Father is God, the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God; yet there are not three Gods, but one God.

The three creeds serve distinct purposes: the Apostles’ Creed summarises Christian belief; the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed safeguards the Son’s and Spirit’s full deity within the confession of one God; and the Athanasian Creed defines that confession more precisely.

None claims to exhaust the mystery of God. Each seeks to prevent the mystery from being falsely simplified.

Creeds and the Bible

At this point, a thoughtful Christian may object: if Scripture is sufficient, why do we need creeds? Does later language suggest that the Bible was inadequate?

The concern is legitimate: the Church must never place human words above God’s word. Councils can err, traditions harden into habits, and religious institutions use orthodox language to protect their power.

History gives us no licence for naïveté. The choice, however, is not between having Scripture and having interpretation. It is between interpretation that is acknowledged and interpretation that stays hidden.

Even the person who says, “I have no creed but the Bible,” has formed judgments about what the Bible means. Those judgments may be sound or unsound, but they do not cease to function as a creed merely because they are unwritten.

A faithful creed makes its interpretation visible and therefore testable. It says, in effect: this is what we understand Scripture to teach; examine our confession by the text from which it claims to arise.

Its proper posture is not that of a judge delivering sentence upon Scripture, but of a witness required to answer faithfully to it.

Another objection points out that the word Trinity does not appear in the Bible. That is true, but the absence of a later summary term does not prove the absence of the reality it names.

Scripture does not need to contain every word by which its teaching may be accurately described. The decisive question is whether the term gathers the biblical evidence faithfully or imposes a foreign idea upon it.

The Church may develop precise doctrinal language in response to new questions, without altering the truths revealed in Scripture. The distinction is between clarifying what biblical revelation already teaches and introducing beliefs that cannot be sustained by its testimony.

The same principle applies to words such as person and essence. They are not inspired replacements for biblical speech, nor do they expose the inner life of God to complete human inspection.

They are instruments used with caution. Essence guards the truth that there is one God. Persons guards the truth that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not merely three names for one temporary role.

The language is valuable only while it serves the revelation it was fashioned to protect.

Some will object that creeds have been used to exclude, condemn or silence. The objection has force. A true confession may be handled with a false spirit. Precision without humility can become cruelty, and the defence of doctrine can be corrupted by ambition.

Abuse, however, does not remove rightful use. The fact that a court may misuse a statute does not make law unnecessary; it makes faithful judgment more urgent. In the same way, the misuse of a creed calls the Church back to truth, charity and submission to Scripture.

The creeds are neither outdated statements of little value nor infallible additions to Scripture. They help Christians across generations express and preserve the central truths of their faith. Their authority remains subordinate to Scripture, against which their teachings must always be tested.

Guides, Not Authorities

The creeds do not enlarge God’s revelation or confer truth upon Scripture. They trace, in disciplined language, the contours the Church has found in the biblical witness.

Where a creed speaks truly, its authority is derivative. Where any human confession departs from Scripture, Scripture must prevail.

Their subordinate place is the source of their dignity.

A trustworthy witness does not become less valuable because the events to which he testifies are greater than himself. His honour lies in telling the truth about what he has received.

The creeds have endured because the questions they address cannot be escaped. Empires have disappeared and intellectual fashions have passed, but Christians must still ask: Who is Jesus Christ? Is the Holy Spirit truly God? How can we worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit while confessing one God?

Every generation may use different language around those questions, but none can make them unimportant.

Nor can the Church safely imagine that old errors stay buried in old centuries. The names may change while the instincts return.

We may speak highly of Jesus but hesitate to confess Him as fully God. We may speak of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit as though they were only different ways in which one solitary person presents Himself. We may divide the works of God so sharply that the unity of the Godhead is obscured.

Ancient controversies still matter because the desire to simplify God persists. The creeds restrain it by showing where plausible shortcuts depart from Scripture. They do not settle every question. They mark which answers give up what God has revealed.

Such restraint is wise: mystery is not contradiction, nor humility a refusal to think. The doctrine of the Godhead requires the Church to think carefully, speak clearly and stop where revelation stops.

The Truth Preserved

The story of the creeds is not the story of the Church inventing a difficult doctrine and placing it upon the shoulders of later believers.

It is the story of the Church receiving a revelation it did not author, encountering interpretations that threatened to diminish it and learning to confess its faith more exactly.

God spoke. Scripture preserved the authoritative witness to His self-disclosure. The Church listened, worshipped, argued, corrected and confessed. At its best, the creedal tradition is the record of that listening.

We need not pretend that every council was free from politics, every theologian from pride or every defender of orthodoxy from failure. The truth of the Godhead does not rest upon the perfection of those who defended it. It rests upon the God who revealed Himself and the Scriptures by which every defence must be judged.

The creeds did not give us a God to believe in. They sought to keep the Church from exchanging the God of revelation for a God of its own convenience.

Possessing this truth is one thing; knowing the God to whom it points is another.

sections.title: When Knowing About God is not Enough
sections.html:
The Distance Between Knowing and Living

People can understand a principle accurately while living at a considerable distance from it. A lawyer may explain justice persuasively and still pursue an advantage that troubles his conscience. An employer may affirm human dignity while treating the people who work for him as though their usefulness exhausts their worth.

The difficulty goes beyond professional conduct. We may understand the importance of family while giving it whatever attention is left after ambition has taken its share. We may recognise the limits of wealth while continuing to expect financial success to settle questions it has never been able to answer.

These discrepancies do not always arise from ignorance. Sometimes we possess the relevant knowledge, can defend it when questioned and sincerely believe it. When the principle becomes inconvenient, another conviction appears to govern us instead.

What kind of knowledge do we possess when we can explain a truth while staying untouched by it? Has something failed in our understanding, or have we understood and then resisted what we know?

The question matters within Christianity because familiarity with God can appear to answer it prematurely. We know the language, recognise the passages and understand what our tradition teaches. Those accomplishments may be valuable without establishing that we know the God to whom they refer.

Scripture is the authority, and the historic creeds are witnesses to the truths received from it. We must now ask what happens when that testimony becomes familiar.

Does possessing true information about God establish acquaintance with Him? And how could a thoughtful reader determine whether “knowing God” means anything more than believing strongly in an idea?

These questions should concern believers and unbelievers alike. A secular reader may have encountered enough religious profession to doubt that it reaches anything real. A Christian may have become so accustomed to that profession that its meaning seldom receives examination.

We should also distinguish acquaintance from consistency. A person may truly know someone and still disappoint him, misunderstand his wishes or resist a rightful claim. Failure in conduct does not, by itself, establish the absence of relationship.

Nor does admirable conduct prove a person’s knowledge of God. People without Christian faith may display courage, generosity and integrity, while Christians may behave shamefully. The enquiry cannot be settled through a simple comparison of moral performance.

The concern is this: whom do we believe we know, upon what grounds, and what place does that knowledge occupy in our understanding of life?

Jesus gives the Christian claim its deepest expression:

“And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.” John 17:3

Within that claim, knowledge of God concerns the Father and the Son whom He has sent. It goes beyond religious vocabulary into a relationship upon which life itself depends.

Before asking what knowing God changes, we must understand what Christians mean when they say that He can be known.

When Familiarity Becomes a Substitute

Familiarity can make a subject feel settled before it has been understood. Words heard repeatedly become easy to recognise, and recognition can produce confidence that their meaning no longer requires attention.

Legal practice offers a useful illustration. An organisation may possess a carefully drafted constitution defining its purposes, responsibilities and procedures. Its officers may know the document, invoke it during disagreements and require new members to acknowledge its authority.

The organisation’s actual decisions may still be governed by patronage, fear or convenience. The constitution stays visible while the habits determining conduct develop elsewhere.

The difficulty is deeper than an occasional breach. The document’s continuing presence may reassure everyone that the organisation still operates according to its principles. Possessing it becomes evidence of faithfulness, even where its authority is seldom permitted to disturb an attractive decision.

The members may therefore need more than another copy. They need to examine what they have accepted, what it requires and why other considerations have acquired greater practical authority.

Religious familiarity can produce a similar reassurance. A person recognises the name of God, knows the accepted answers and participates comfortably in Christian conversation. Those signs can be mistaken for evidence that the God being discussed occupies the place the confession assigns to Him.

A Christian may affirm that God is Creator while treating life as though its purpose were entirely self-determined. He may confess divine holiness while expecting God to approve whatever he has already decided. The words stay recognisable, but their meaning has been adjusted.

Sometimes no deliberate adjustment occurs. Attention simply drifts towards immediate demands, and truths once considered deeply become background language. A person continues to believe while giving very little thought to the One believed in.

This danger extends beyond religious belief. Someone may dismiss Christianity because it seems familiar from childhood, public controversy or disappointing encounters with Christians. Familiarity can discourage genuine enquiry on either side.

Neither inherited acceptance nor inherited dismissal removes the need to examine what is actually being claimed. We may know enough religious language to feel confident while knowing too little of its meaning to judge it fairly.

Scripture repeatedly exposes this problem among people who possessed considerable religious privilege. Israel knew the name of the God who had delivered them, received His commandments and lived within a history shaped by His acts. Familiarity did not prevent them from misunderstanding His character or resisting His purposes.

Their information had value. The danger was that possession of the testimony could become a substitute for attending to the God who had given it.

The creeds preserve distinctions that are still necessary. They help the Church recognise when familiar words have acquired meanings the biblical testimony cannot sustain. Their usefulness depends upon readers continuing to ask what they confess.

A creed cannot trust God on our behalf. Its words can guide our understanding, but each generation must receive the truth towards which they point.

Familiarity becomes dangerous when it gives us permission to stop listening. We cease to ask whether our understanding is still answerable to the One whom we claim to know.

Knowing About God and Knowing God

The distinction between possessing information and knowing a person came into focus for me during a professional encounter. Before meeting me, a contractor knew certain public facts about my life, including my profession and my role within the Foundation.

He may also have encountered information about my background online. Had we passed one another on the street, however, neither of us might have recognised the other.

After we met and spoke at length, those facts had acquired another setting. He had encountered something of my manner, priorities, temperament and convictions. Information about me had become connected to the person to whom it belonged.

One conversation did not disclose everything. He could still misunderstand me, discover something unexpected or revise an impression formed too quickly. Still, the acquaintance was real, though incomplete.

The distinction is familiar in other relationships. A biography may give us extensive knowledge of someone we have never met, while a child may truly know a parent without understanding much of that parent’s history. The quantity of information and the existence of acquaintance are related without being identical.

Applied to God, the illustration requires restraint. My contractor met a visible person and heard him speak in an ordinary conversation. The encounter explains a distinction between kinds of knowledge; it does not establish that God exists or prove that a claimed relationship with Him is authentic.

It does, however, help us ask a clearer question. If God is personal and has made Himself known, would collecting statements about Him exhaust the knowledge that His revelation makes possible?

Christianity answers by presenting God’s self-disclosure as a summons to trust the One disclosed. The testimony tells us whom we are approaching, what He has done and what He promises. Receiving it involves more than becoming competent in describing its contents.

J. I. Packer made this distinction central to Knowing God (1973). Theology matters because it teaches us whom we confess, and its intended movement carries the reader towards the God of whom it speaks. Accurate understanding should deepen personal knowledge rather than become a substitute for it.

Four distinctions must therefore be held together. Information concerns what we know about God; acquaintance concerns the One to whom that information refers. Trust concerns our response to Him, while conduct reveals something of how that trust is being expressed or resisted.

These cannot be collapsed into one test. A believer’s failure may expose disobedience within a real relationship, and a difficult season may weaken confidence without making God unknown. Equally, fluent religious speech can conceal the absence of personal trust.

Knowing God requires neither constant emotion nor perfect consistency. It requires receiving Him as real: His truth corrects us, His promises invite trust and His authority exceeds our preferences.

Christ’s words expose the possibility of stopping short:

“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” John 5:39–40

The sacred testimony was present, and its subject was being examined. Yet Christ identified a refusal to come to the Person to whom it pointed.

Religious study itself can therefore become a means of maintaining distance. We may analyse a message, organise its teachings and defend its authority while postponing the question of what it asks of us.

This warning falls first upon those who honour Scripture. Intellectual seriousness is a virtue, but it gives us no exemption from the claim of the truth we study. Theology is conducted before the God whose identity it seeks to understand.

Can We Really Know God?

A secular reader may reasonably press the contractor illustration further. “I understand how someone came to know you: he met you and spoke with you. How does anyone know God, and how could that knowledge be distinguished from imagination or religious conditioning?”

The question needs more than an appeal to personal certainty. People within different religions may describe deep experiences with equal sincerity. Others may discover that an impression they attributed to God arose from fear, desire or the influence of a trusted community.

Emotional force cannot settle the identity of its supposed source. Comfort or better conduct does not make an experience divine, though such effects are worth weighing.

Christianity locates the beginning of knowledge elsewhere: in God’s initiative to make Himself known. As Chapter Two argued, the claim concerns His words and acts, recorded in Scripture and brought to their decisive expression in Jesus Christ.

A questioning reader may still dispute that testimony. This chapter clarifies what the Christian account means and which substitutes for knowing God fall short.

Christians do not mean that inward feelings reveal a God of their choosing. They mean that the God revealed in Scripture can be personally trusted and approached, while their understanding stays answerable to His revelation.

Within Christian life, this involves attending to Scripture, considering its meaning, addressing God in prayer and responding to what He has disclosed. Christians understand the Holy Spirit as enabling that reception; His work does not make the identity of God whatever an individual happens to experience.

These practices are not a mechanical procedure for producing an encounter. Their significance depends upon the truth of the testimony and the reality of the God addressed.

Personal knowledge often depends upon what someone makes known about himself. God has done so through His words and acts, decisively in Jesus Christ. Our question here is whether receiving that testimony means only understanding its contents or also trusting the One it reveals.

The Christian account concerns a living God who is still active. It gives the believer no permission to abandon His revealed identity in favour of untested impressions. Personal conviction must stay answerable to Scripture and open to correction in how that Scripture has been understood.

Distortion can occur even where many individual statements are true. A person may know true facts about someone while assembling from them a misleading picture. Selective attention can make affection resemble approval of everything, or authority resemble indifference to suffering.

Our understanding of God can be distorted in the same way. Love detached from holiness may produce a God who never challenges us. Sovereignty detached from goodness may produce a God whose power inspires fear without trust.

The resulting picture may feel familiar and contain biblical language. Its adequacy depends upon whether it receives the whole testimony rather than protecting a preferred selection.

Believers must therefore face a question as serious as the one they put to sceptics: are we responding to the God who has revealed Himself, or to a convenient picture assembled from our expectations?

Real knowledge permits correction. If nothing God reveals can unsettle our assumptions, our confidence may concern a protected idea rather than the living God.

Incomplete understanding need not make knowledge impossible. Christianity claims that God can be known truly while being beyond exhaustive comprehension. The right response joins confidence in what He has disclosed with humility about what we have not understood.

The Light by Which We See

What difference, then, does knowing God make? God can no longer be confined to religious occasions while the rest of life draws its meaning and direction from elsewhere.

This conviction underlies the practical questions explored in later chapters. It shapes how we understand ourselves, relate to others and make sense of the world around us. To know the Creator is to see creation in the light of its Source.

Our achievements may remain valuable without becoming the measure of our worth. We may struggle to understand others without denying them the dignity they possess. And even when painful experiences remain unresolved, we need not conclude that life has no greater purpose simply because we cannot yet discern it.

These changes in perspective do not promise immediate moral perfection. We do not always live by what we know, and believers remain capable of selfishness, confusion and serious wrongdoing. Understanding brings responsibilities that may require time, humility and sometimes painful correction.

We return, then, to the difficulty raised at the beginning of this chapter. Understanding a truth, knowing a person, trusting him and living faithfully are not quite the same thing. Knowing God brings them together, even if the distance between what we believe and how we live does not disappear overnight.

The image of light helps us understand why this matters. Daylight is not another object in the landscape; it allows us to see everything else more clearly. In much the same way, knowing God sheds light on a world whose existence and meaning already depend upon Him.

This does not explain every tragedy or provide ready answers to life's difficult decisions. Rather, it gives us a clearer perspective from which to consider creation, human dignity, responsibility and hope. We continue to ask questions and seek understanding, but with a growing awareness that the world we investigate cannot be separated from its Creator.

Familiarity with religious language is not the same as knowing God. We may believe sincerely and still be mistaken, just as a belief may offer comfort without being true. The strength of our conviction cannot establish the truth of what we believe. What matters is whether our understanding reflects who God truly is.

And if knowing God changes how we understand everything else, we must begin not with the God we imagine, but with the God who has revealed Himself.

Who is this God whom we are called to know?

sections.title: Part II
sections.subtitle: Meet The Triune God
sections.html:
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.” Matthew 28:19

We have asked why knowing God matters, how He reveals Himself and whether knowing about Him is the same as knowing Him. Those questions bring us to His identity. Who is the God we are called to know?

The expression knowing God can easily become vague. It may describe religious sincerity, moral conviction, spiritual experience or a general belief that some higher power exists. None of these, by itself, identifies the God whom Scripture calls us to know.

God is not known by assigning Him the character we would prefer Him to possess, or by reducing Him to the attributes our culture finds easiest to accept. We must attend to who He has revealed Himself to be.

The Christian answer goes further than saying that God is powerful, eternal, holy, righteous and loving, although He is all these and infinitely more. Scripture presents the one living and true God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Matthew’s account of Christ’s command brings those names together within a single act of discipleship. Christians are to baptise in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. What does that command teach us about the God whose name they bear?

We look first at the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as Scripture presents them: what each says and does, and how they are distinguished. Why can the Father and the Son not be treated as mere roles, or the Holy Spirit as an impersonal force?

We then ask how the Church can confess the three while affirming that there is one God. What does it mean to call them personally distinct yet undivided in the divine being? Some explanations clarify the confession. Others achieve simplicity by overlooking part of the evidence.

The confession must also face scrutiny: the strongest objections from those outside the Christian faith, and from Christians troubled by its language or implications. Can the doctrine answer them fairly while remaining faithful to Scripture and honest about the limits of human explanation?

These are questions about the identity of the God whom Christians worship. The purpose is neither to reduce Him to a formula nor to shelter difficult claims behind the word mystery. It is to examine what He has made known about Himself, and to resist explanations that preserve one part of the biblical witness by surrendering another.

Before considering His works and how His presence shapes our lives, we must settle who He is.

We begin with the Triune God Himself.

sections.title: The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Beyond Familiar Names

At the beginning of Jesus’ public ministry, the Gospels bring the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit before us within a single scene.

The Son stands in the waters of Jordan. The Spirit of God descends like a dove. The Father speaks from heaven:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Matthew 3:17

This is no abstract definition and no later theological construction. The Father speaks, the Son is baptised and the Holy Spirit descends. The three are personally distinguished within a single scene.

Christians speak of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit because this is how God has made Himself known. We pray to God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, worship Him as such, and baptise in obedience to Christ using those very names.

Their familiarity is a blessing, and also a danger. Words repeated often enough may be accepted without being weighed.

The Bible’s answer to the question of God is simple and mysterious at once. The One who created all things has revealed Himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

These are not three gods. Nor are they three temporary roles assumed by one divine Person at different moments in history. The Church did not invent this truth. It encountered it in Scripture, confessed it and handed it from one generation to another.

This chapter has a modest purpose. It does not attempt to exhaust the mystery of the Godhead. No chapter could.

It examines the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as Scripture presents them. The next chapter will consider how the three Persons are truly distinguished without dividing the one God.

Before we explore what the Triune God does, we must first understand who He has revealed Himself to be.

The Father

The Bible begins deliberately. It does not begin by explaining God. It begins with God.

Before there is a universe to describe, humanity to create or history to unfold, there is God. He is never presented as One whose existence depends upon proof or human acceptance. He is the eternal reality from whom every other reality proceeds.

Moses writes:

“In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.” Genesis 1:1

Everything begins there.

The opening verse of the Bible establishes the relationship between God and everything else. He is the Creator; everything else is created. The universe is neither self-existent nor self-explanatory. It owes its origin and continued existence to the God who called it into being.

Creation is the undivided work of the Triune God. Scripture will disclose the Son as the One through whom all things were made and the Holy Spirit as present and active in creation. The Father is therefore not a solitary Creator acting apart from the Son and the Spirit.

As the biblical story unfolds, the one God is revealed as the covenant Lord who calls, promises, delivers and remains faithful. He calls Abraham and promises that through him all the families of the earth will be blessed. He hears Israel’s cry in Egypt, remembers His covenant and brings His people out of bondage.

At Sinai, God does not begin by demanding that Israel earn deliverance. He declares:

“I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.” Exodus 20:2

Obedience follows deliverance. It does not purchase it.

That covenant faithfulness continues through Israel’s judges, kings and prophets. God promises David a kingdom and a throne established for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). The promise reaches beyond David’s lifetime and awaits its ultimate fulfilment in Jesus Christ.

The prophets call a wandering people back to the God who has not abandoned His word. Jeremiah announces a new covenant in which God will write His law upon the heart and remember His people’s sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34).

The Old Testament therefore reveals the one God as Creator and covenant Lord. It also anticipates divine Fatherhood.

God calls Israel His son (Exodus 4:22). He asks through Malachi, “Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?” (Malachi 2:10). Concerning David’s royal heir, He promises, “I will be his father, and he shall be my son” (2 Samuel 7:14).

These passages prepare the ground, but the eternal identity of the Father comes into its clearest light through Jesus Christ.

The God who possesses all authority makes Himself known through the language of relationship without surrendering any part of His holiness or majesty. Jesus teaches His disciples:

“After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven...” Matthew 6:9

Those words give the believer’s approach to God a new intimacy. The Creator of heaven and earth is neither distant nor indifferent towards His people. Through Christ, believers may approach Him with the confidence of children who know the love, faithfulness and care of their heavenly Father.

We must nevertheless distinguish two related truths.

God is eternally the Father of the Son. He did not become Father when the world was created or when Jesus was born in Bethlehem. The Son speaks of the glory He shared with the Father “before the world was” (John 17:5), revealing a relationship that precedes creation itself.

Believers are children of God in another sense. We are not divine by nature, nor do we enter the eternal Son’s unique place. We are adopted by grace through Christ:

“...ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.” Romans 8:15

His Sonship is eternal and essential; ours is received and gracious.

Some modern readers hesitate before the title Father because human fatherhood has often been distorted by absence, cruelty or domination. That concern is fair, but the biblical order must not be reversed.

God is not called Father because He resembles the failures of earthly fathers. Earthly fatherhood is answerable to the perfect love, authority and faithfulness revealed in Him.

Nor does the title imply that God is biologically male. Scripture declares that God is Spirit (John 4:24), beyond the bodily limitations of human sex.

Father is nevertheless not a disposable metaphor chosen by culture. It is the name by which the Son reveals and addresses Him, and it identifies the eternal relationship between the Father and the Son.

That fatherly love is seen most clearly in His purpose to redeem fallen humanity. Jesus declares:

“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son...” John 3:16

Salvation begins with the Father’s initiative. Before humanity sought Him, He loved; before anyone believed, He gave.

Redemption is not an attempt by the Son to persuade a reluctant Father to become merciful. It is the outworking, through the Son, of the mercy the Father had already purposed.

The New Testament repeatedly presents the Father as the One who sends. He sends the Son into the world, and He sends the Holy Spirit in the Son’s name. The Son likewise speaks of sending the Spirit from the Father (John 15:26).

This order reveals personal distinction and the gracious movement of God towards us. It does not imply that the Son or the Spirit is inferior in divine nature.

The Father is also described as the One “of whom are all things” (1 Corinthians 8:6). Scripture reveals an order in the relations and works of the divine Persons, but never a hierarchy of deity. The Father is not more God than the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor does He act independently of them.

To know the Father is therefore to know far more than the first Person named in a Christian formula. He is the eternal Father of the Son, the Author of redemption and the Father who adopts believers by grace.

The Father sends the Son and gives the Holy Spirit to His people. These are not three separate divine projects, but the ordered and undivided work of the one God.

The Son, Jesus Christ

The New Testament makes an astonishing claim: in the eternal Son, God Himself entered human history.

Every major religion remembers remarkable teachers. History honours leaders whose influence has shaped nations and generations. Christianity certainly recognises Jesus as a teacher, but it refuses to stop there.

If He were merely an exceptional man, His life would deserve admiration but not worship. The Christian faith stands or falls on the greater claim that in Jesus Christ, God has made Himself known.

John begins his Gospel with words that deliberately return the reader to Genesis:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” John 1:1

John is not introducing a new God. He is revealing the eternal Son who existed before creation. The One who would walk the roads of Galilee, speak beside the sea and suffer upon the cross is the eternal Word through whom all things were made.

A few verses later, John records the moment that changed human history:

“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us...” John 1:14

The Incarnation stands at the centre of the New Testament’s claim. God did not merely send another prophet. In the eternal Son, God Himself entered the world He had made.

Without ceasing to be fully God, the Son assumed our humanity and entered the ordinary realities of human life. He knew hunger, weariness, sorrow, rejection and suffering. He lived among the people He had created, not only to reveal the Father but ultimately to reconcile humanity to Him.

The Gospels direct our attention beyond Christ’s miracles to His identity. His works reveal who He is.

Jesus declares:

“I and my Father are one.” John 10:30

Within John’s Gospel, these words contribute to a cumulative testimony that Jesus is more than a religious teacher. They do not identify Him as the Father: the same Gospel records the Son speaking to, coming from and returning to the Father.

Nor can the word one, considered alone, settle every question concerning the divine nature. Christ later prays concerning His disciples:

“That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee...” John 17:21

John has already told us that the Word was both “with God” and “was God” (John 1:1). Personal distinction and deity stand together in the same sentence.

At the other end of John’s Gospel, Thomas stands before the risen Christ and confesses: “My Lord and my God.” John 20:28
