“Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?” Matthew 6:26

His words do not dismiss the needs that make us anxious. They direct us to the Father who knows those needs and cares for His children.

Trust does not make planning unnecessary or guarantee that every desired outcome will arrive. It teaches us to distinguish the responsibilities we must fulfil from the control we do not possess.

We can prepare, work diligently and seek help where it is needed. We cannot ensure every result, prevent every loss or carry the future by thinking about it constantly.

The Father’s care, the Son’s advocacy and the Spirit’s indwelling presence give the believer grounds for confidence within that limitation. We are responsible, but we are not alone.

Communion with God grows through prayer, Scripture, worship, repentance and fellowship. These ordinary practices teach us to listen, bring Him our concerns without pretence and respond to what He reveals.

These practices are not payments made to secure His attention. Their purpose is relationship, and they can become empty routines if we perform them while refusing the trust and obedience they invite.

Spiritual maturity is therefore not measured by dramatic experiences alone. It may appear in a willingness to pause before reacting, seek God’s direction before deciding or entrust an unresolved concern to Him before resting.

The believer gradually learns to live in the awareness of God’s abiding presence, even when that presence is neither felt nor immediately apparent.

Transformation Is Not Arrival

The God who reconciles us to Himself also works to make us more like His Son. His presence brings comfort and assurance, but it also brings to light attitudes, desires and habits we might otherwise prefer to leave unchanged.

This transformation is genuine, but it does not happen all at once. Believers continue to face temptation, personal weaknesses and the lingering influence of habits formed over many years.

We may trust God sincerely and still lose patience under pressure. Having received mercy, we may struggle to show it to others. Even when we believe we have overcome certain fears or resentments, we may be surprised by how easily they return.

These struggles are neither reasons to surrender to despair nor excuses to remain as we are. Rather, they invite us to examine ourselves honestly, turn again to God and depend more fully upon the grace that continues to transform us.

Paul writes:

“But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.” 2 Corinthians 3:18

The passage describes believers being changed through the work of the Spirit. Their attention is directed towards the Lord, whose likeness the Spirit is forming within them.

Legal practice offers a useful distinction. A judgment may change a person's legal standing immediately, but it does not necessarily change that person's character, habits or way of life.

The Gospel addresses both our standing before God and the life we are called to live. Through faith in Christ, we are justified before God, while the Holy Spirit continues to shape our character, desires and conduct to reflect the Saviour to whom we now belong.

Justification and sanctification are therefore distinct, but inseparable. We do not earn God's acceptance through a lifetime of moral improvement. Rather, the grace that receives us also begins the work of transforming us.

Confusing these truths can lead us in opposite directions. We may treat every failure as evidence that God has rejected us, or take His acceptance as permission to resist the very changes His grace calls us to make.

The believer, then, has every reason to rest in God's grace and every reason to continue growing. Repentance is not an attempt to earn His acceptance, but a response to the relationship we have already received.

Often, the need for repentance becomes apparent in ordinary situations. We discover that truths we readily affirm have not always shaped our words, our handling of money or our response to someone who has wronged us.

It is here that transformation becomes practical. An apology may be overdue, a dishonest practice must end, a grievance needs reconsideration or a neglected responsibility demands attention.

The Holy Spirit does not remove our responsibility to act. He enables us to respond, working through Scripture, wise correction and even uncomfortable circumstances that bring hidden weaknesses into the open.

Spiritual growth is not always easy to measure. Its evidence may emerge gradually: a greater willingness to admit wrongdoing, more patience under pressure, deeper compassion for others and less inclination to excuse familiar sins.

These changes, however, require honest examination. Feeling sorry is not necessarily the same as repentance, and the promise of gradual growth must never become an excuse for refusing to change.

At the same time, our imperfections need not obscure the progress already made. We can acknowledge how far we still have to go while recognising, with gratitude, what God has begun to accomplish within us.

Transformation is not arrival. It is the continuing work of God's Spirit, shaping those who belong to Christ into lives that increasingly reflect Him.

When Meaning Is Not Felt

There are seasons in which the believer cannot readily see what God is doing. Circumstances remain painful, prayer appears unanswered and the assurances once spoken confidently become difficult to feel. What does fellowship with God mean then? How do we trust Him when we cannot explain what He has permitted?

Scripture does not require us to disguise anguish. Its prayers of lament give believers words for experiences that cheerful assurances cannot meet.

David asks:

“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” Psalm 13:1

He brings his bewilderment to God. The question expresses the distress of someone who continues to seek Him, even while experiencing what feels like abandonment.

Christ’s sorrow in Gethsemane also prevents us from treating distress as evidence of spiritual failure. He was “exceeding sorrowful, even unto death,” and asked that the cup might pass from Him while yielding to the Father’s will (Matthew 26:38–39).

Trust and anguish can dwell in the same heart. Faith does not always ease the pain of suffering or provide words to explain it away. Sometimes, faithfulness simply means continuing to pray, even when the heart is heavy and answers seem distant.

When my father died in April 2023, my belief in the Resurrection did not make his absence any less painful. I believed in the promise of eternal life before his passing, and I held to that same promise afterwards. But knowing that death had been conquered did not spare me the sorrow of losing someone I loved so deeply.

What faith changed was not the reality of my grief, but my understanding of its finality. Death could bring profound sorrow, but it could not extinguish the hope secured through the Resurrection of Christ.

Christian hope does not promise an explanation for every sorrow or an immediate end to suffering. It offers something more enduring: the assurance that, however deeply death may wound us, it does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.

The Holy Spirit helps us where we cannot express that trust.

Paul writes:

“Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought…” Romans 8:26

We are not required to produce eloquent prayers before we can seek God. Our weakness is among the conditions in which the Spirit helps us.

Nor must we carry every difficulty privately. Other believers, wise counsel and professional help can be part of the support through which God sustains us.

God’s presence is not measured by the strength of our emotions or the favourability of our circumstances. Faith can remain genuine even in seasons of deep sorrow, when prayers come with difficulty and hope seems barely within reach.

We may not understand why certain things happen, nor find answers that adequately explain our pain. But we can still turn to God, bringing our questions, fears and sorrows before Him, trusting in His presence without pretending to understand what He has not revealed.

A Different Way of Living

Fellowship with God changes how believers treat the people around them. What we confess about Him must increasingly shape what others encounter in us.

Paul writes: “And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind…” Romans 12:2

Renewal touches thought, motive, speech and conduct. Its significance becomes especially clear when obedience costs something we would prefer to keep.

Honesty is tested when concealment offers an advantage. Mercy becomes difficult when another person has acted unfairly, and humility is needed when success makes correction unwelcome.

These pressures arise in homes and workplaces as much as in public life. A believer’s character is revealed in how employees are paid, disagreements with a spouse are handled and those without influence are treated.

Legal and commercial practice particularly expose the gap between what is permitted and what is right. An action may be lawful without being wise, fair or consistent with our professed responsibilities.

Christian faith does not remove the need for firmness. A lawyer may pursue a lawful remedy, a business owner may enforce an agreement and a parent may impose necessary discipline.

The question also concerns how these responsibilities are exercised. Truth need not be delivered with contempt, authority need not become intimidation and the pursuit of justice need not be governed by revenge.

The believer will not always manage this well. Failure calls for more than an appeal to good intentions; it may require an apology, restitution or a change in conduct.

Grace makes us willing to face that responsibility. Protecting our reputation becomes less important than addressing the wrong we have done.

Christ declares: “Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.” Matthew 5:14

This image gives Christian living a visible expression in the world. People encounter our faith not merely through what we say, but through how we conduct ourselves, especially when we have fallen short.

Professing faith alone cannot sustain that testimony. Claims of Christian identity carry little weight when dishonesty, cruelty or pride are repeatedly excused or defended.

Credibility, however, does not demand perfection. It calls for the humility to acknowledge our failings, the willingness to accept correction and the resolve to live by what we profess. Genuine repentance often speaks more powerfully than any claim to righteousness.

The testimony of our lives, then, takes shape in the ordinary responsibilities of each day. Through integrity, patience, courage and love, others may begin to recognise something of the God whose grace continues to transform us.

Hope in Every Season

Fellowship with God also transforms how believers face the uncertainties of the future. Christian hope is not built upon the assurance that life will always improve or that difficulties will eventually disappear. It rests upon something far more enduring: the Resurrection of Christ and the promise of life secured through Him.

Peter writes:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” 1 Peter 1:3

This hope gives us something more enduring than confidence in our plans. We may wait, experience disappointment and reach the end of a season without the result for which we prayed, but the risen Christ remains the ground of our expectation.

Comparison can quietly undermine the confidence that Christian hope gives us. We begin to measure our careers, families, opportunities and achievements against what we see in the lives of others, often forgetting how little of their full story we truly know.

We see their successes, but rarely the struggles behind them. And in measuring what we have against what others appear to enjoy, we risk losing gratitude for our own blessings, simply because someone else seems to have received more, or arrived there sooner.

Agriculture offers a reminder. One farmer may plant maize or cassava and gather a harvest within a relatively short period. Another plants palm trees and waits through years in which the land appears to offer little return.

Several shorter harvests may be gathered while the young palms are still being cleared around, protected and patiently tended. When the palms reach maturity, however, they may produce for decades.

A palm farmer therefore has little reason to envy the maize farmer. The crops are different, their seasons are different and comparison ignores the purposes they serve.

The illustration has limits. Faith does not guarantee that waiting will eventually produce greater wealth, public recognition or the outcome we preferred.

Some losses remain losses within this life. Some acts of obedience receive little acknowledgement, and some hopes we have cherished must be surrendered.

Christian hope can withstand those realities because its foundation lies beyond them. Christ’s Resurrection directs us towards the fulfilment of God’s saving promise, not merely the eventual success of our present ambitions.

This frees us to value faithfulness where results are modest or unseen. Caring for a dependent relative, keeping an unwelcome promise or refusing a dishonest advantage may bring no recognition, but visible reward is not the measure of their worth.

We can still plan, work and pray. Hope teaches us to do so without making a particular outcome the condition upon which we continue to trust God.

A season of waiting need not be interpreted as divine rejection. Another person’s progress need not become an accusation against our own life.

The Father remains faithful, the Son’s saving work remains sufficient and the Spirit continues to sustain those who belong to Him. Our future rests upon God’s promise rather than our ability to predict its course.

Hope therefore strengthens responsibility. It enables us to work without surrendering to envy, endure disappointment without abandoning trust and receive success without making it the purpose of our lives.

From the Believer to the Church

Life in fellowship with the Triune God touches identity, prayer, character, suffering, conduct and hope. These are the places where knowledge of Him becomes part of the life we actually lead.

The believer remains a person in need of grace. Growth includes correction, and faithfulness includes returning to God when we have failed.

Such a life was never intended to develop in isolation. We need others who will help us understand Scripture, recognise what we overlook, bear burdens we cannot carry alone and practise the love we profess.

Fellowship also places responsibilities upon us. We are called to offer the patience, truth and care that we ourselves need to receive.

Through Christ, believers belong to one Father and share in the life given by one Spirit. Their relationship with God brings them into relationship with one another, across differences of background, circumstance and experience.

God is forming a people who worship Him, grow together and bear witness to His grace. The renewal of individual lives therefore leads us towards the community in which those lives are joined.

We turn now to the Church and the life it is called to share.

sections.title: In the Church and Her Ministry
sections.html:
The Family God Is Still Building

The longer I have observed the Church, the more convinced I am that she cannot be understood apart from the Godhead. Her identity and calling arise from the God to whom she belongs.

If we see the Church merely as another religious institution, we shall judge her by human standards. Attendance, programmes, buildings and finances may have their place. None explains why she exists.

Long before congregations or denominations, there was the eternal fellowship of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Through Christ and by the Spirit, the Church has been brought into communion with the Father. Paul writes:

“For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father.” Ephesians 2:18

This fellowship does not mean that believers become divine or share in God's essence. The distinction between Creator and creation remains. Rather, those once separated from God are graciously welcomed into communion with Him and, through that same grace, brought into fellowship with one another.

Paul continues:

“Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God.” Ephesians 2:19

The Church is more than a gathering of people who share the same beliefs. She is a family brought together by grace, united not merely by what her members profess, but by the God to whom they belong. She is the household of the Father, the body and bride of the Son, and the temple of the Holy Spirit: one people called into fellowship with the Triune God and with one another.

I sometimes think about this belonging while sitting at the back of a church auditorium. Before the service begins, I watch acquaintances greet one another, parents settle their children and others sit quietly in prayer.

Some arrive expectant; others carry unseen burdens. As the service begins, people whose lives differ in many ways turn together towards God in reverence.

Watching them reminds me that shared interests or backgrounds cannot explain this gathering. Jesus Christ brings us together and teaches us to receive one another as members of His family.

A harder question follows. If God remains present in His Church, how do we account for the failures, divisions and abuses within her? Do these shortcomings reflect upon God, or upon those through whom He works?

Jesus declares:

“I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” Matthew 16:18

It is His Church, and He builds her. Christ does not hand that responsibility to institutions or personalities. Nor does His promise guarantee the faithfulness of every congregation or minister.

The Church’s history includes serious failures. Communities proclaiming reconciliation have been divided by rivalry, while institutions established to serve have sometimes protected themselves at others’ expense.

Spiritual authority has been misused. Manipulation, prejudice, commercialisation and concealed wrongdoing have wounded people within communities that should have offered compassion, truth and spiritual succour.

Such failures cannot be excused as ordinary human imperfection. The secular critic who points to hypocrisy may be right to do so, and those who were harmed must be listened to, not silenced.

The failures of the Church must never be mistaken for failures of the God she professes to serve. Dishonesty, exploitation and abuse do not reflect His character; they betray the holiness, justice and love revealed in Scripture.

This distinction, however, offers the Church no refuge from accountability. Those who bear God's name, especially those entrusted with spiritual authority, remain answerable to the very God they claim to represent.

Consider Corinth. Paul addressed a congregation troubled by divisions, immorality and disorderly worship. He nevertheless called them “the church of God” (1 Corinthians 1:2), while firmly confronting their conduct.

God had neither abandoned them nor ceased to correct them. They remained in need of His transforming grace.

Similarly, the risen Christ warned the church at Ephesus that its candlestick could be removed unless it repented (Revelation 2:1–5). His continuing authority includes the right to correct and judge His Church.

Christ’s faithfulness to His Church must never be mistaken for unquestioning approval of everything done in His name. Genuine repentance may demand the admission of wrongdoing, the surrender of abused authority and the courage to place truth and human dignity above institutional reputation.

The Church, however, cannot be defined solely by her failures. Across generations, countless believers have lived out their faith through quiet acts of service, steadfast devotion and compassionate care for the vulnerable, often without recognition or reward. Their lives bear testimony to the grace that continues to work within her.

In Life Together, Dietrich Bonhoeffer warned against the temptation to love an idealised Christian community more than the people God has given us. Fellowship requires grace and patience, but never tolerance of abuse.

The Church is unfinished. That explains her condition; it does not excuse it. Christ continues to sanctify her, looking towards the day when He will present her to Himself “a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27).

That promised condition remains ahead. The Church is still being formed, called to reflect God’s character while needing His correction and transforming grace.

The Father has not forsaken His household, the Son has not relinquished His Church, and the Holy Spirit has not ceased His work among God’s people. Their continuing work confronts the Church’s imperfections instead of hiding them.

The Church is the family God is still building. Her failures must be confronted because she belongs to Christ, and her hope endures because the Triune God remains faithful to the work He has begun.

Gathered in God’s Presence

Worshipping together is one of God’s gifts to His people. In gathered worship, believers give expression to a belonging that extends beyond personal experience.

Private worship nurtures personal communion with God. Corporate worship reminds believers that they belong to a people whose life does not begin or end with individual experience.

Few people arrive at worship with completely uncluttered minds. Some celebrate answered prayers. Others carry financial pressure, illness, disappointment or burdens they have shared with no one.

Outwardly, we appear as one congregation. Inwardly, each person carries a story known fully only to God.

Those individual stories gradually yield to a common act of worship. Distraction gives way, however imperfectly, to attention. Private concerns are placed within the larger reality that we have gathered before the living God.

The Psalmist writes:

“O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together.” Psalm 34:3

Another person’s prayer may give language to a burden we could not express, and the public reading of Scripture may steady a heart unsettled all week.

We come both to receive and to participate. Our prayers and voices contribute to the worship of a people among whom others may be weary or newly learning to trust God.

The burdens we bring into worship do not always disappear when the service ends. Financial pressures, illness and difficult responsibilities may still await us, even after heartfelt prayers and songs of praise.

Worship, however, can change how we face these realities. It lifts our attention beyond our immediate concerns and reminds us that the God we worship is greater than our circumstances, steadfast in His care and sovereign in His authority.

Through the Son and by the Holy Spirit, the Church draws near to the Father, enjoying the access Christ has secured and the fellowship His redeeming work has restored.

James K. A. Smith has emphasised that worship forms more than our understanding. Its prayers, songs and repeated practices also shape what we love.

What we sing, hear and proclaim in worship therefore matters deeply. These repeated expressions of faith shape our understanding of God, either drawing us closer to the truth of His character or reinforcing expectations that Scripture does not support.

Gathered worship is more than an opportunity to gain knowledge or enjoy an uplifting experience. It draws our hearts towards God, shaping what we desire, strengthening our devotion and reminding us where our ultimate allegiance belongs.

Online worship can be a genuine blessing, especially for those prevented by illness, travel or distance from gathering in person. Neither physical separation nor the limits of technology can prevent God from reaching and sustaining His people.

Where gathering is possible, however, watching a service cannot fully replace the fellowship of believers. The life of the Church involves more than receiving a message. It calls for shared presence, mutual encouragement and practical care for one another.

Worshipping the Father, Son and Holy Spirit

The language of Christian worship can initially appear confusing. One song addresses the Father, another is directed to Jesus and a prayer invokes the Holy Spirit.

Are Christians worshipping one God, or moving between several divine figures? The answer lies in the confession examined in the earlier chapters.

Christians worship the one God revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Addressing the Son does not identify Him as the Father, and invoking the Spirit does not treat Him as an atmosphere generated by the gathering.

These personal distinctions remain real within the unity of God. Worship should honour them without suggesting that the Church directs separate portions of devotion towards three independent gods.

The New Testament frequently presents prayer and worship as directed to the Father, through the Son and in the Holy Spirit. This pattern expresses the relationship into which believers have been brought.

It is not a rigid rule forbidding worship addressed to the Son or the Spirit. The Church acknowledges the full deity of each without erasing the distinction between them.

Gordon Fee emphasised the New Testament’s presentation of the Spirit as God’s personally experienced presence. This reminds the Church that His place in worship is more than a name in a doctrinal statement.

He sustains the fellowship of God’s people and directs them towards Christ. His work is not measured by emotional intensity, though true worship may stir deep feelings.

Good worship joins understanding to devotion. It honours the distinctions between Father, Son and Holy Spirit and worships the one God.

The Word, Baptism and the Table

The Church is nurtured and strengthened through the practices Christ has entrusted to her. Through them, she is continually drawn back to the Gospel that gave her life, reminded of the grace that sustains her and called to live faithfully by the truth she proclaims.

Through the reading and preaching of Scripture, the Church is instructed, challenged and corrected by the Word of God. She is called to proclaim its enduring truths amid changing circumstances, remaining faithful to the Gospel she has received rather than claiming authority to reshape its message.

Paul writes:

“So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” Romans 10:17

Preaching requires more than speaking confidently about a religious subject. Its task is to open Scripture faithfully and proclaim Christ, so that those who hear can understand and respond.

The preacher also stands under that truth. Authority in teaching does not place anyone beyond the correction of the Word being taught.

Baptism identifies people with Christ and marks their reception into the visible fellowship of His Church. Jesus commands:

“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.” Matthew 28:19

Christians differ about baptism’s proper subjects, mode and precise theological meaning. These disagreements matter, but they should not obscure its place within Christ’s command and the Church’s shared confession of the Triune God.

At the Lord’s Table, the Church remembers Christ’s sacrifice and proclaims the saving power of His death. As Paul declares:

“For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come.” 1 Corinthians 11:26

Christian traditions differ in their understanding of Christ’s presence at the Table, but the meal directs believers to His sacrifice, invites honest self-examination and affirms a fellowship that must find expression in how they treat one another.

The Table also points beyond remembrance to the hope of His return. The words “till he come” remind us that the Saviour whose death we proclaim is also the risen Lord whose coming we await.

Through the Word, baptism and the Lord’s Table, the Church continually bears witness to the Gospel she has received, remembering what Christ has accomplished and renewing her commitment to live in the light of His grace.

Fellowship: Grace Among Imperfect People

Christian fellowship becomes especially important when life grows difficult. Disappointment and loss show how much care God provides through the prayers and presence of His people.

Many burdens remain unseen. A person may attend church while carrying concerns about a marriage, a struggling business or the health of someone dearly loved.

Those nearby may never know every detail. They can nevertheless offer a relationship in which help may be sought without shame and received without becoming a public spectacle.

Paul writes:

“Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” Galatians 6:2

Burden-bearing requires attention. We cannot support people well if our fellowship never moves beyond greetings or if every admission of difficulty is met with hurried advice.

Care may be a visit, a meal or financial help. It may mean listening, praying or simply staying beside someone when words offer little comfort. Such care grows from the unity God has given believers in Christ. Paul writes:

“There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all…” Ephesians 4:4–6

The Church is called to reflect in everyday life the fellowship Christ has established. Her members need not agree on every preference or perspective to recognise their shared responsibility to love, support and care for one another.

The strength of this fellowship cannot be measured by attendance figures or public prominence alone. A large congregation may still leave individuals feeling isolated, while a smaller community may demonstrate remarkable spiritual maturity through genuine relationships, faithful service and mutual care.

Christ prayed:

“That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us…” John 17:21

Believers do not become one divine being. Their shared allegiance and love bear witness to the God who has gathered them.

The strength of this fellowship becomes especially evident where differences might otherwise have kept people apart. Age, ethnicity, profession and wealth should never determine whose burdens deserve attention or whose contributions are valued.

Such fellowship calls for humility. People from different backgrounds may challenge assumptions we have long accepted, while those who correct us may reveal weaknesses we have failed to recognise in ourselves.

Receiving correction is not always easy, and offering it requires wisdom and care. Genuine concern must never become an excuse for expressing personal irritation under the appearance of spiritual responsibility.

Forgiveness does not mean ignoring wrongdoing, nor does love require abandoning healthy boundaries. Reconciliation must uphold truth, protect the vulnerable and never pressure those who have suffered harm to return to unsafe relationships.

Fellowship matures where grace is both received and extended, where truth is spoken with love and where people remain committed to one another's good.

Ministry Beyond the Pulpit

The knowledge of God finds practical expression in service. Peter writes:

“As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.” 1 Peter 4:10

The gift is received, and its use is entrusted. Ministry begins with stewardship rather than a claim to personal importance.

Some believers are called to preach, teach or hold recognised offices within the Church. Their work should be honoured and supported, but ministry belongs to the whole body.

I have gradually found my own place in service mostly outside the pulpit. Law, administration, enterprise, humanitarian work and Christian literature have become the settings in which what God has entrusted to me can benefit others.

This has broadened the question I ask about vocation. Alongside What have I been enabled to accomplish? stands another: How can what has been entrusted to me become a blessing?

That question applies to every believer. Ability, experience and time can all be placed in the service of Christ, including where no formal ministry title is attached.

It also examines our motives. Work performed in God’s name can still become a means of securing recognition or a sense of our own significance.

Paul writes:

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” Ephesians 2:10

Salvation is not a reward for human effort, but a gift of God's grace received through faith in Christ. That same grace transforms the believer, finding expression in a life increasingly marked by love, obedience and faithful service to others.

The lawyer who pursues justice, the administrator who acts with integrity and the entrepreneur who treats employees fairly all have opportunities to honour Christ through their work. So too do the parent nurturing a child and the farmer whose labour helps sustain others.

Excellence and integrity are essential to such service. Good intentions cannot justify negligence, just as professional achievement can never excuse dishonesty, exploitation or cruelty.

The Church’s ministry does not end with the closing prayer. Her members carry their faith into their homes, workplaces, farms and schools, where everyday responsibilities become opportunities to honour God through faithful service.

The Holy Spirit gives different gifts to members of the Church, enabling them to support and strengthen one another. No one possesses every gift, and the importance of a contribution is never determined by how visible or celebrated it may be.

Much of this service takes place quietly, away from public recognition. A word of encouragement, a patient act of kindness or consistent care may sustain someone whose struggles remain unknown to others.

The Church honours God when she recognises, nurtures and supports these expressions of faithful service.

Witness: Receiving and Handing on the Faith

No generation invents the Christian faith. Each receives a testimony through Scripture, teaching and the lives of those who have gone before.

That inheritance brings responsibility. It must be examined faithfully and handed on without distortion.

Paul writes to Timothy:

“And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.” 2 Timothy 2:2

The sentence runs across four links: Paul, Timothy, faithful men and those they will teach. Each receives something meant to be passed on.

I understand that responsibility personally. Much of what first formed my knowledge of God came through the teaching and example of my late father, whose writings on the Godhead helped inspire this book.

Receiving an inheritance does not end the need for enquiry. We must return to Scripture to test what we have received, then say it plainly in our own generation.

The work of the Foundation and the writing of these books form part of that responsibility. Literature and humanitarian service are ways of placing what has been received at the service of others.

The Church is called to proclaim Christ beyond her fellowship, reaching those unfamiliar with Him, mistaken about His Gospel or alienated by Christian conduct.

Service can make the Church’s love tangible, but it cannot by itself explain the Gospel. People must also hear who Christ is, what He has accomplished and His call to repentance and faith.

Words and conduct belong together. Compassion cannot replace proclamation, and proclamation cannot excuse conduct that contradicts it.

The Church’s mission proceeds from God’s saving initiative. The Father sent the Son, and the Spirit empowers believers to bear witness to Him. The Church serves a purpose she has received rather than one she has invented.

The theologian Lesslie Newbigin described the Church as a sign, instrument and foretaste of the kingdom of God.

These descriptions remind us that the Church is not herself the kingdom. Her life points towards God's reign, her proclamation and service advance His purposes, and her fellowship offers a glimpse of the reconciliation He has promised. Her imperfections, however, reveal that she still awaits the fullness of what she proclaims.

When the Church speaks truthfully, welcomes those often overlooked and challenges the abuse of power, her actions lend credibility to her message. People are more likely to take her proclamation seriously when they see a community genuinely seeking to live by the teachings of the Lord she professes.

Such a calling requires both courage and humility. The Church must proclaim her faith with conviction while remaining willing to listen, understand and engage thoughtfully with those she seeks to reach.

We cannot determine how others will respond to the Gospel or how future generations will receive it. Our responsibility is to live it faithfully and pass it on with integrity.

Awaiting Her King

The Church serves in the present and waits for the future God has promised. Her hope gives her present work direction.

Paul writes:

“For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ.” Philippians 3:20

The Church’s highest allegiance belongs to Christ. She is called to care deeply about the world’s suffering and participate responsibly in its affairs, without losing sight of the greater purpose towards which God is directing history.

This hope does not require a complete understanding of biblical prophecy. Christians have sometimes allowed genuine expectation to become misplaced certainty, making confident claims about dates and events that Scripture has not clearly revealed.

The Church is called not to speculation, but to watchfulness and faithful living. The times and seasons remain within the Father’s authority. Our responsibility is not to predict what He has withheld, but to live faithfully by what He has revealed.

The closing pages of Scripture give the Church a prayer that has echoed through generations:

“Even so, come, Lord Jesus.” Revelation 22:20

The Church awaits the Lord who redeemed her and continues to sustain and build her. His promised return is the great hope towards which her worship, service and testimony are directed.

Until that day, she must remain faithful to her calling while recognising her continuing need for correction and renewal. Hope in Christ must never become an excuse for complacency about the condition of His people.

Her testimony remains imperfect because those who make up her fellowship are still being transformed. But her ultimate hope rests not upon their perfection, but upon the faithfulness of the God whose grace brought her into being.

We have traced the work of the Triune God from creation, through redemption, to the life of the Church. One final movement remains: the fulfilment of all that He has promised.

The God who began the story will also bring it to its appointed fulfilment.

sections.title: Part IV
sections.subtitle: The Consequence of Knowing God
sections.html:
“Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done...” Isaiah 46:10

Isaiah’s words place the future firmly within God’s knowledge and authority. We make plans and pursue our ambitions, but none of us can see the full course of our lives, much less the destination towards which history is moving. What, then, does it mean to know the God who declares the end from the beginning?

Knowledge changes how we understand and experience life. Knowing the destination of a journey gives meaning to the steps along the way. Understanding someone better transforms how we relate to them. Knowing God carries implications far greater than either.

We have explored why this knowledge matters and examined how God has revealed Himself in Scripture. We have considered the confession of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, confronted serious objections and traced the work of the Triune God from creation through redemption to the life of the Church.

Our enquiry now turns towards the future. If the God we have come to know is Creator, Redeemer and Lord of history, how should that knowledge shape our expectations, our choices and the civilisation we are building?

Chapter Eleven asks what Christian hope permits us to say about the future. What has God promised, and where must we resist claiming more certainty than Scripture gives? If the end of the story belongs to Him, how should we live before it comes?

Chapter Twelve turns to the responsibilities we share with others. If every person bears a dignity received from God, what claims does that truth make upon leadership and the use of power? As technology and artificial intelligence enlarge human capability, what wisdom should govern what we choose to build?

These questions belong together. Human beings raise families, pursue careers and shape institutions, and their decisions may outlast them. We act within a future we cannot fully see, while bearing responsibility for what we place into the hands of the next generation.

The knowledge of God offers no exhaustive account of tomorrow and no ready answer to every decision. It still requires us to ask where history is going and what kind of faithfulness the present demands.

We turn first to the future, not to escape the present, but to discover how God’s promised tomorrow should change the way we live today.

sections.title: Living Today in the Light of Tomorrow
sections.html:
The Future That Changes the Present

Human beings have always sought to understand what the future holds. Indeed, much of prudent living involves anticipating what lies ahead and preparing wisely for it.

We make financial projections, prepare succession plans and study political trends. Increasingly sophisticated tools help us predict weather, assess risks and anticipate markets.

Preparation does not, however, give us control. A transaction may be overtaken by an unforeseen event, a business plan may encounter conditions no model predicted and a family may face a change for which no one was ready.

Careful planning has served me well. It has never guaranteed an outcome.

Christian hope answers our inability to control the future with God’s promise: history is neither unknown to Him nor beyond His government.

That promise does not give believers advance knowledge of every circumstance. It gives them grounds for trust while circumstances are uncertain.

If history is moving towards God’s appointed purpose, what difference should that confidence make to the way we live while it is still unfolding? Peter asks with particular urgency:

“Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness?” 2 Peter 3:11

In the King James Version, conversation means conduct or manner of life. Peter shifts attention from what believers expect to who they ought to become.

That question governs this chapter. Prophecy, resurrection, judgment and new creation concern our present choices because they reveal the future towards which those choices are made.

God’s promised future gives present responsibilities their proper measure. We may labour diligently without requiring temporary achievements to supply ultimate meaning, and face disappointment without assuming that every unfinished purpose has been wasted.

Tomorrow belongs to God. That assurance calls us to live faithfully today.

The Future We Cannot Master

Biblical prophecy gives us reason to trust in God's purposes, not to presume that we can unravel every detail of His timetable.

Human forecasting draws upon available evidence to anticipate what might happen. Prophecy, by contrast, concerns what God has chosen to reveal about His purposes. Understanding it requires humility, careful attention to Scripture and the wisdom to distinguish what God has disclosed from what we merely assume.

The first coming of Christ illustrates why this distinction matters. Israel had received genuine promises concerning the Messiah, but their full meaning was not always understood before the events they foretold unfolded.

Many expected a deliverer who would overcome Israel’s enemies and restore the kingdom. The possibility that the promised Messiah would first suffer, face rejection and die was far more difficult to reconcile with those expectations.

From the perspective of the Cross and Resurrection, Christians can recognise connections that were less apparent beforehand. The fulfilment of these prophecies revealed not only the faithfulness of God's promises, but also the limits of human understanding in anticipating how those promises would be fulfilled.

We face a similar danger when we become so convinced of our interpretations that we no longer allow Scripture to challenge them. Sincerity alone does not guarantee that our conclusions are correct.

Wars, political upheavals, natural disasters, technological advances and economic crises are often linked to particular biblical prophecies. Such connections may deserve careful consideration, but plausible interpretations must never be presented as established truths without sufficient biblical grounds.

Where God has spoken clearly, we can stand with confidence. Where interpretations remain disputed or details have not been revealed, humility is not a weakness of faith, but an expression of it.

Isaiah writes:

“Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.” Isaiah 46:10

The assurance rests upon God’s counsel. Its fulfilment does not depend upon our ability to identify every stage in advance.

The passage of time raises another question: if Christ promised to return, why does His coming seem so long delayed? Peter records the objection:

“Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation.” 2 Peter 3:4

The difficulty is real. Generations of Christians have watched, waited and died without witnessing the return they expected.

Does that waiting weaken the promise? Peter answers by directing attention to the patience of God:

“The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.” 2 Peter 3:9

Peter reminds us that apparent delay reflects God's patience. His faithfulness cannot be measured by human expectations of when His promises should be fulfilled.

The passage offers no date or timetable. Instead, it reveals something far more important about God's character: His patience extends the opportunity for repentance, not an invitation to complacency.

Christian watchfulness, then, is not about calculating when the end will come. It is about examining how we live, responding to God's mercy and remaining faithful in the responsibilities entrusted to us.

We may not know when history will reach its appointed fulfilment, but we can trust the God who has promised to bring it there.

The Future God Has Promised

If Scripture does not disclose every detail of the future, what does it clearly promise? Christ will return, the dead will be raised, humanity will face judgment, evil will be finally defeated, and God will dwell with His people in a renewed creation.

These promises give Christian hope its substance and certainty. The future is not merely the passage of time towards an unknown destination, but the fulfilment of God's redemptive purpose and the establishment of His righteousness over all creation.

John writes:

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away…” Revelation 21:1

The One seated upon the throne then declares:

“Behold, I make all things new.” Revelation 21:5

The biblical story moves towards the fulfilment of God's purpose for His creation. Sin, suffering and death have profoundly wounded the world, but none will determine its final destiny.

Christians differ in their understanding of how the present creation relates to the new. Scripture speaks of judgment and dissolution, but also of liberation and renewal. These descriptions call for humility, particularly where interpretations attempt to explain more than the biblical passages disclose.

Whatever the precise nature of this transformation, the central promise remains clear. God will overcome the corruption that has wounded His creation and dwell among His people.

Christian hope, therefore, embraces bodily resurrection and life in a creation made new. It is not simply the escape of the soul from physical existence, but the restoration of life according to God's purpose.

This expectation also gives us reason to care for the world we inhabit. The promise of future renewal does not excuse present neglect, waste or destruction. What God has made remains worthy of responsible stewardship.

The future also brings accountability. Christ will judge the living and the dead. Evil will not escape His judgment, nor will wealth, influence or earthly power place anyone beyond His authority.

Believers themselves are not exempt from accountability. Paul writes:

“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ…” 2 Corinthians 5:10

Paul speaks here of the lives and conduct of those who belong to Christ. What we do matters before Him, including choices, actions and motives that may never become known to others.

Salvation is received through faith in Christ, not purchased through good works. But the grace that saves us does not make our conduct unimportant or remove our responsibility to live faithfully.

This truth should lead us to honest self-examination rather than eagerness to condemn others. The One who judges is also the Saviour who gave Himself for sinners, and none of us stands before Him without need of mercy.

A sceptical reader may, at this point, regard these promises as comforting ideas developed to ease humanity's fear of death. Such an objection deserves serious consideration, for Christian hope must rest upon something more substantial than the desire for a reassuring future.

The apostolic proclamation rests upon the claim that Jesus Christ truly rose from the dead. Paul acknowledges the consequences plainly: if Christ has not risen, Christian faith is vain (1 Corinthians 15:14–17).

Christian hope, then, stands upon a claim about what God has accomplished in history, not merely upon what humanity wishes to believe. If Christ is risen, His Resurrection provides the foundation for trusting the future He has promised.

That future also brings the work of the Triune God to its appointed fulfilment. The Father accomplishes His eternal purpose, the Son brings His redemptive victory to completion, and the Holy Spirit prepares God's people for the inheritance awaiting them. Paul writes:

“Then cometh the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father…” 1 Corinthians 15:24

He continues:

“And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all.” 1 Corinthians 15:28

Paul describes the completion of Christ's mediatorial reign, not any loss or diminishment of His deity. The Son delivers the kingdom to the Father, having brought to fulfilment the saving mission for which He came.

This does not mean that Christ ceases to reign or that His place within the Godhead changes. Scripture's final vision places “the throne of God and of the Lamb” at the very centre of the renewed creation (Revelation 22:1–3).

The Holy Spirit's work in believers also points towards this promised future. Paul describes Him as:

“…the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession…” Ephesians 1:14

The word earnest refers to a pledge or guarantee. The Spirit's presence is therefore not merely a blessing for the present life, but an assurance of the inheritance believers will one day enjoy in its fullness.

The future does not introduce us to a different God or an unfamiliar purpose. It reveals the completion of what the Father has intended, the Son has accomplished and the Holy Spirit continues to bring to fulfilment.

These promises also speak directly to how we live today. If God's justice will ultimately prevail, we cannot remain indifferent to injustice around us. If death will be defeated and creation renewed, human life and the world entrusted to our care must never be treated as disposable.

The certainty of God's promised future does not diminish the importance of the present. It gives our choices, responsibilities and faithfulness a significance that reaches beyond our own lifetime.

What Tomorrow Requires of Us Today

We return to Peter’s question: “What manner of persons ought ye to be?” The answer must become visible in how believers use their time, fulfil responsibilities and respond when obedience carries a cost.

Legal work, enterprise, family care and community service retain their importance when placed against eternity. Their value lies partly in the people they affect and the opportunities they provide to serve faithfully.

A legal matter may determine a family’s livelihood. A business decision may affect employees and their dependants, while a community project may continue meeting needs long after its founders are gone.

Future hope teaches us to take these consequences seriously. The people affected by our decisions are not instruments of our ambition; they are persons whose lives matter before God.

Sometimes faithfulness requires accepting a loss. A professional may refuse a profitable instruction because it requires dishonesty, even when another opportunity is neither visible nor guaranteed.

The worth of that refusal does not depend upon a better offer arriving tomorrow. It rests upon obedience to Christ, whose judgment reaches beyond the immediate result.

Outcomes still matter: a favourable judgment is preferable to an unjust one, and a useful project should be planned and managed so that it fulfils its purpose.

Visible success, however, cannot become the final measure of faithfulness. Some obedient work bears fruit that another generation will gather; some is interrupted or receives little recognition.

Christ’s Resurrection prevents believers from treating apparent defeat as necessarily final. It gives us grounds for perseverance without excusing poor judgment or careless work.

Christian hope also gives us courage to face uncertainty and adversity. If death does not have the final word, fear need not determine our choices. Believers can speak truth, stand against injustice and bear the cost of obedience, trusting in God's sustaining grace even as they recognise their own weaknesses and continuing need for His help.

Patience belongs to the same confidence. Not every wrong is corrected immediately, and not every prayer receives the answer desired. The God who holds the end may still be trusted within the unfinished middle.

Peter’s question also directs us towards holiness. The future God promises is a life in which evil has no place; expecting that future should deepen our willingness to resist evil now.

Such expectation requires humility. We know what God has promised because He has made it known, and that knowledge gives us no grounds for contempt or certainty about matters He has left undisclosed.

Jürgen Moltmann’s Theology of Hope (1964) drew attention to the active character of Christian expectation. Hope challenges acceptance of conditions that contradict God’s promised future and calls believers to act within the present.

That action must stay within its limits. Politics, technology, philanthropy and moral effort cannot accomplish the new creation; its fulfilment belongs to God.

They can still become settings for responsible service. Christians may pursue just arrangements, develop useful tools, relieve suffering and protect vulnerable people without imagining that human achievement can complete redemption.

Every act of reconciliation reflects something of the peace God has promised. Upholding human dignity and extending mercy demonstrate allegiance to the King whose judgments are righteous and whose compassion reaches those who suffer.

Such actions, however, do not replace the proclamation of Christ. The hope that shapes Christian conduct also gives believers a message worth sharing and a responsibility to invite others into the salvation He offers.

We live between what Christ has already accomplished and what God has promised to fulfil. Christ has risen, but death remains a present reality. Redemption has been secured, but creation still groans under the weight of corruption. The Holy Spirit has been given, but the fullness of our inheritance still awaits us.

Believers live confidently in what God has begun while awaiting what He has promised to complete. This waiting is neither passive nor purposeless. It embraces work, worship, repentance, service and faithful testimony, all directed towards the Lord who will bring His redemptive purpose to fulfilment.

One fundamental question remains: what does knowing God mean for the civilisation we are building?

Our age possesses extraordinary knowledge and unprecedented power. Whether we have the wisdom to use them rightly is the question to which our enquiry now turns.

sections.title: The Godhead and the World Ahead
sections.html:
More Knowledge, Less Understanding

We return to the question this book began with. Our powers of explanation, production and influence now exceed those of earlier generations, but they have not necessarily given us greater clarity about the ends they ought to serve.

We must now consider what this knowledge means for the civilisation we are building. How should knowing the Triune God influence our use of technology, our exercise of authority and our understanding of what it means for humanity to flourish? As our power to shape the world grows faster than our agreement about how it should be used, what principles should guide our choices?

Knowing God does not provide ready-made answers to every scientific, legal, economic or political question. Rather, it gives us a foundation from which to examine those questions, consider their consequences and judge whether our achievements serve the deeper purposes for which human life was created.

The world we are building will demand discovery, expertise and sound judgment. But it will also need people who understand why truth must be upheld, why every human life deserves dignity and why the power to accomplish something does not necessarily give us the moral right to pursue it.

These concerns lie at the heart of our enquiry into the Godhead. The world owes its existence to the Father, through the Son and by the life-giving power of the Holy Spirit. Creation is the undivided work of the one God. It is neither a world without an Owner nor a possession humanity is free to exploit without restraint.

The incarnation brings this truth into the very heart of human history. The eternal Son entered the world He created, revealing God's holiness and love through a truly human life. His compassion for the overlooked, His refusal to use power for personal glory and His obedience even unto death challenge every notion of greatness built upon privilege, dominance or self-interest.

The Holy Spirit carries this truth into the human heart. His transforming work addresses the distance between knowing what is right and having the will to do it. Civilisation may develop increasingly powerful tools, but no advancement in technology can, by itself, close that moral distance.

Understanding the world remains essential to human progress. Knowing God gives us a deeper foundation for recognising its worth, exercising our growing powers responsibly and understanding the limits of what we ought to pursue.

Power in Search of a Purpose

Human progress has brought benefits for which we should be grateful. Disease can be prevented or treated, information crosses continents in moments, and education reaches people whom distance or circumstance once excluded. Christians have reason to welcome discoveries that relieve suffering and deepen understanding of God’s world.

The difficulty begins when increasing capability is treated as evidence of increasing wisdom. A society may become more efficient while becoming less just, or acquire new powers before deciding what obligations should govern them.

Artificial intelligence brings these questions into focus. A system may help an institution assess applications for employment or credit, processing information at a speed no individual could match. Its usefulness, however, does not settle who is responsible for the decisions made through it.

Take an applicant refused an opportunity because an automated assessment classifies him as unsuitable. The officer points to the system, the institution points to its supplier, and the supplier explains that the institution determined how the system would be used. The person affected still needs an answer.

Responsibility has passed through several hands without necessarily being accepted by any of them. Delegating part of a decision does not remove the obligation to explain it, examine its fairness and correct an injustice.

The deeper moral question, then, is not simply what a machine can do, but who determines what it should do. Whose interests does it serve, whose rights does it protect, and what recourse is available when its use causes harm? No increase in computing power can, by itself, supply the moral principles needed to answer these questions.

Human dignity must remain inviolable amid such advances. Our worth neither increases with productivity nor diminishes with dependence. An infant, an elderly person and someone living with a severe disability possess the same inherent dignity, regardless of their abilities, achievements or perceived usefulness.

Christian faith grounds this dignity in humanity's creation in the image of God. By taking on human nature, the eternal Son further reveals the value God places upon the humanity we are sometimes tempted to measure by achievement or usefulness. No person should become expendable simply because technology can accomplish a task more efficiently without them.

Technology also amplifies the intentions of those who wield it. Pride, greed, prejudice and the desire for control are longstanding human weaknesses. In the hands of increasingly powerful systems, their consequences can reach further, affect more lives and cause harm on a far greater scale.

The Tower of Babel offers an ancient illustration of this danger. Its builders possessed remarkable ambition, organisation and collective ability. Their intentions, however, were revealed in their own words:

“Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name…” Genesis 11:4

Their ambition was not merely to build something impressive, but to establish their own greatness. The deeper lesson lies not in the height of the tower, but in the pride that inspired it. Human achievement becomes dangerous when the pursuit of greatness loses sight of the God to whom humanity remains accountable.

Modern civilisation builds with different tools, but must confront much the same temptation. What are we ultimately seeking through our achievements, and what are we willing to sacrifice in their pursuit? An undertaking may demonstrate extraordinary intelligence while revealing a deeply inadequate understanding of what is good.

A secular reader may reasonably point out that moral understanding is not confined to religious belief. Reason, experience and concern for human welfare can also inform our judgments. Secular thinkers have offered serious accounts of human dignity grounded in our shared humanity, rational capacities or objective moral truths, without making that dignity dependent upon public approval.

These perspectives deserve thoughtful engagement. The Christian conviction, however, is that human dignity rests upon something no government or institution has created: every person bears the image of God. Governments may recognise, uphold and protect that dignity, but they possess no authority to take away the worth from which it arises.

This distinction becomes especially important when popular approval is treated as sufficient justification for an action. Agreement may strengthen a just decision, but no majority can transform wrongdoing into righteousness simply by endorsing it.

Religious communities are equally accountable to this standard. Invoking God's name does not make an action right, nor does religious conviction place anyone beyond moral examination. What we profess must be reflected in purposes and conduct consistent with His revealed character.

The civilisation we are building needs more than technological brilliance. It needs the moral wisdom to govern its achievements and the humility to recognise that our growing power remains answerable to truths we did not create.

Leadership, Law and Stewardship

The way we exercise authority reveals much about how we value those entrusted to our care. Citizens may be regarded as people to be served, employees as individuals whose dignity and interests deserve respect, and institutions as trusts to be responsibly managed. Equally, they may be reduced to instruments for advancing personal ambition.

The Christian understanding of authority places every position of power beneath the sovereignty of God. No ruler bestows human dignity upon those he governs, and no institution possesses an unlimited right to determine the worth, freedom or moral obligations of those under its authority.

Paul writes:

“For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.” Romans 13:1

Government therefore has a rightful place in the ordering of human society. But the legitimacy of an office does not make its occupant divine, nor does it render every exercise of authority morally justified.

When the apostles were commanded to abandon the work God had entrusted to them, their response was unequivocal:

“We ought to obey God rather than men.” Acts 5:29

Respect for authority must therefore be accompanied by an understanding of its limits. Every office carries responsibilities as well as powers, and those entrusted with authority remain accountable for how they exercise both.

Christ expresses the true measure of leadership in words that challenge every ambition for power:

“Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.” Matthew 20:27

In the life of the eternal Son, we encounter authority exercised through service, without compromising truth or overlooking wrongdoing. His example challenges every leader to look beyond the privileges of office and consider a more searching question: whose interests does my authority truly serve?

This understanding of leadership finds its deepest expression in the work of the Triune God. The Father sends the Son, the Son fulfils His mission in loving obedience, and the Holy Spirit transforms believers into the likeness of Christ. Their united work reveals a pattern of authority and service that human ambition alone cannot provide.

My experience in law and enterprise brings these principles into everyday practice. Every transaction demands careful attention to rights, obligations, evidence and enforceability. But responsible professional judgment must also consider the fairness of the arrangement and the dignity of those affected by it.

Consider an agreement that satisfies every formal legal requirement. Its signatures may be valid, its terms clearly expressed and its obligations enforceable. But what if those terms take unfair advantage of another person's desperate circumstances? The fact that an agreement can be enforced does not necessarily establish that those seeking to enforce it have acted honourably.

Commercial firmness has its rightful place, and not every unfavourable bargain amounts to injustice. Distinguishing legitimate advantage from exploitation requires careful judgment, not hasty moral condemnation. It also challenges the professional adviser to look beyond what a client can lawfully obtain and consider what fairness and integrity may require.

Law remains indispensable to an orderly society. It protects rights, restrains wrongdoing, establishes procedures and provides remedies when obligations are breached. In doing so, it shapes conduct, reinforces expectations and encourages respect for established standards.

But law cannot, by itself, transform the human heart. Rules may prevent certain abuses while leaving the desire to exploit others untouched. People may comply with the letter of the law while searching for new ways to secure the very advantages its principles were intended to restrain.

A sound institution therefore needs safeguards and people willing to honour their purpose. Accountability must be strong enough to restrain wrongdoing, while character must be formed deeply enough to sustain faithful conduct when scrutiny is absent.

The Church is equally bound by these principles. She cannot credibly condemn secrecy, exploitation or the abuse of authority in society while allowing the same practices to flourish within her own institutions. Her testimony carries weight only when she is willing to live by the truth she proclaims.

Christians may reasonably disagree about public policies, constitutional structures and the proper limits of government. Such questions demand careful examination, reliable evidence and sound judgment. Knowing God does not relieve us of the responsibility to understand the complexities involved.

It establishes moral obligations beyond political or personal advantage. Truth must be upheld, the vulnerable protected and opponents treated with dignity. Authority is not merely a privilege, but a sacred trust for which those who exercise it must ultimately give account.

What Human Flourishing Requires

Law, commerce, science and government fulfil different functions, but each touches human lives. Their achievements must therefore be measured not only by what they accomplish, but also by how they affect the people whose lives they shape.

An employee is more than a source of productivity. A client is more than a legal dispute, and a community is more than the location of a successful project. Behind every professional or institutional decision are people whose dignity exists independently of the value others place upon them.

This understanding gives stewardship practical meaning. Profit can create jobs, encourage investment and provide resources for generosity. Professional success can open greater opportunities to serve others. Both are legitimate pursuits, but they lose their moral direction when the desire for achievement or advantage makes us indifferent to the harm others may suffer.

Justice and mercy must also be held together. In God, neither diminishes His holiness nor compromises His love. The Cross reveals both the gravity of sin and the extraordinary depth of divine grace.

Our pursuit of justice must therefore confront wrongdoing without losing compassion for those involved. Equally, mercy must never come at the expense of those who have suffered harm. It must make room for truth, accountability, protection and, where possible, meaningful restoration. Compassion loses its moral force when it overlooks the very suffering it is meant to address.

Human flourishing also depends upon the material conditions that allow people to live with dignity, security and opportunity. Access to healthcare, quality education, essential infrastructure and meaningful economic opportunities is vital. Poverty is neither a virtue to be romanticised nor suffering a condition to be passively accepted. Where hardship can be prevented or relieved, compassion must find expression in practical action.

Prosperity alone cannot guarantee a fulfilling life. Greater wealth and freedom of choice may coexist with strained relationships, while professional success may leave us struggling to find rest, trust others or give generously. Even communities with impressive infrastructure and modern conveniences may gradually lose the relationships and shared values that hold them together.

Christ asks:

“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” Mark 8:36

His question makes us examine the end towards which achievement is directed. What have we gained if the pursuit of success destroys the life it was intended to enrich?

The Godhead gives human flourishing a meaning that reaches beyond wealth, achievement and personal success. We owe our existence to the Father's creative generosity, are called into reconciliation with God through the Son, and are transformed by the Holy Spirit into people capable of deeper love, faithfulness and self-control. These truths speak to dimensions of human life that prosperity and technological progress alone cannot satisfy.

Their significance becomes apparent in everyday decisions. Will an employer conceal a known danger to protect profits? Will a professional adviser remain silent when truth threatens a client's advantage? Will a public officer exercise lawful discretion to protect the vulnerable or exploit their circumstances?

Such choices help determine the kind of world we are building. Civilisation depends upon institutions, but institutions are shaped, strengthened or weakened by the people who serve within them. Decisions made far from public attention can have consequences that reach well beyond those who make them.

Human achievement remains valuable, even as its limitations become apparent. Medicine can relieve suffering, law can restrain injustice, and sound economic policies can expand opportunity. Each deserves serious commitment and continued improvement, but none can, by itself, heal the deeper disorder of the human heart.

Christians can therefore pursue excellence without arrogance, embrace progress without making it an object of worship, and acknowledge failure without abandoning the pursuit of what is good. We can learn from others, contribute meaningfully to society and recognise that reconciliation with God and transformation by His Spirit address needs no human institution can ultimately satisfy.

Every human endeavour finds its proper value when we recognise both what it can accomplish and what lies beyond its power. Only God can bear the weight of our ultimate hope.

The Enduring Foundation

The world ahead will confront us with questions we cannot yet imagine or fully anticipate. New discoveries will demand fresh understanding and sound judgment, while familiar human ambitions and weaknesses will find increasingly powerful means of expression.

Through all these changes, the central question of this book remains: Who is God? How we answer it shapes our understanding of the world, our regard for the people who inhabit it and our sense of responsibility for the civilisation we are building.

Christian faith confesses one God, eternally Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The God who created all things is the same God who has acted to redeem humanity and continues to transform His people. Creation, redemption and the hope of final restoration are not separate undertakings, but expressions of His one eternal purpose.

Paul writes:

“For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.” Romans 11:36

These words bring our enquiry together in a profound declaration of origin, dependence and purpose. Everything we seek to understand owes its existence to God, remains sustained by His power and finds its ultimate meaning in relation to Him.

Knowing God does not tell the physician which treatment will succeed or the judge which disputed fact has been established. Both must still rely upon evidence, expertise and sound judgment. But knowing Him gives deeper meaning to their responsibilities: why the lives before them matter, why truth must guide their decisions and why professional duty must reach beyond personal interest.

Human knowledge will continue to advance, and even our most carefully reasoned conclusions may require revision. Through every discovery and changing circumstance, the God who revealed Himself to Moses as “I AM” remains the unchanging foundation of all existence (Exodus 3:14).

Our enquiry has brought us to a fundamental conclusion: the world cannot be fully understood merely by explaining how it works. Its existence, its moral demands and its ultimate purpose point beyond themselves to the God upon whom everything depends.

To know God is not to possess every answer. It is to know the One in whom every true answer finds its proper place.

To know Him is to begin to understand everything else.

sections.title: Epilogue
sections.subtitle: Continuing the Odyssey Into the Light
sections.html:
We began with the greatest question humanity can ask: Who is God? We end with a clearer understanding of why the answer reaches into every part of life.

At the beginning of this journey, I suggested that the fact I was writing this book would probably surprise those who know me well. By now, the direction it has taken may be even more surprising. Perhaps it should not be.

Human beings often recognise connections within their lives only in retrospect. Experiences once regarded as unrelated acquire a different significance, while questions pursued separately begin to converge. A purpose may be taking shape before we understand where it is leading.

That is how I now regard this book. I cannot explain every turn my life has taken, but I can recognise connections between experiences, questions and convictions I once considered separately. My father’s death brought many of them into clearer view, but it did not create them; the questions themselves had been gathering for years.

If these pages have helped a reader understand God more clearly, reconsider familiar Christian language or recognise the significance of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, they have served the purpose for which they were written.

Writing them, however, has done something I did not fully anticipate. I began by examining a doctrine. The doctrine gradually began examining me.

The truths considered here went beyond biblical interpretation and theological argument into the ordering of my own life. They have caused me to reconsider the ambitions behind important decisions, the place given to prayer and the ease with which legitimate responsibilities can occupy the attention that belongs first to God.
