Christian writing carries temptations of its own. A work begun as service may become another pursuit of recognition, while a completed manuscript may become an accomplishment to display or an identity to defend.

A book about God cannot exempt its author from His light. I must ask whether these pages direct attention towards Him or, subtly, towards the person whose name appears upon them. That question requires honesty after publication as much as during composition.

The enquiry has also brought greater coherence to my understanding of vocation. Law, enterprise, service and Christian literature involve different duties, but each requires decisions about how life should be ordered within the world God has made.

Even the name Clemesis, adopted for my legal practice many years ago, now carries a significance I did not fully appreciate. It emerged from the tension between clemency and nemesis, mercy and justice, and expressed my desire for firmness without cruelty and compassion without the abandonment of principle.

I now recognise that my desire to hold justice and mercy together pointed towards truths about God I had not yet learned to express clearly.

These responsibilities extend beyond vocation into the generations through which life is received and handed forward. My son will inherit a world markedly different from the one into which I was born. He will encounter possibilities I cannot imagine and dangers I may never live to see.

Odera has gone before me. Akintola will journey beyond me. I stand between inheritance and responsibility, receiving what came before and seeking to entrust something worthwhile to those who come after.

The knowledge of God that sustained my father is more than an heirloom preserved by family memory; it concerns the living, eternal God, whose faithfulness does not diminish as one generation gives way to the next.

I cannot control the world my son will inherit or foresee every question he will face. I can seek to entrust to him something more enduring than achievement, property or reputation: the knowledge of the God in whom every other good inheritance finds its meaning.

This book is part of that stewardship. Its argument now stands complete. Its implications do not.

A book may be completed while the obedience it requires has barely begun. Publication cannot establish whether the truths examined here will become light by which I continue to live; that answer must take shape through choices made beyond these pages.

I have written as one drawn back towards the Source, increasingly aware of truths that have touched my life and responsibilities I must still learn to fulfil. The knowledge of God gives me no standing from which to look down upon others. It calls me into fellowship with the Father, through the Son and by the Holy Spirit.

We enter that fellowship by grace through repentance and faith, and we continue by grace. Whatever truth I have understood was revealed before I discovered it, and whatever faithfulness appears in my life bears witness to God’s patient work within me.

Whatever good these pages accomplish will depend upon the God to whom they point. My hope for the reader is therefore inseparable from my prayer for myself: that neither of us will be satisfied merely to know more about Him.

May the Father who calls us draw us nearer. May our confession of the Son be expressed in trust, love and obedience. May the Holy Spirit expose, cleanse and transform every part of our lives still resistant to His will.

May the knowledge of the Triune God become the light by which we order our lives, fulfil our responsibilities and love the people entrusted to our care.

As for me, I have seen more clearly where the light comes from. I am still learning to walk in it.

The formal exploration now ends. The odyssey into the light continues.

sections.title: Appendix I
sections.subtitle: Key Scriptures of the Godhead
sections.html:
The doctrine of the Godhead rests upon the testimony of Scripture. Christians do not believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three divine Persons because of philosophical speculation or ecclesiastical tradition alone. Rather, this belief arises from the progressive revelation of God throughout the Bible. The Old Testament establishes the absolute unity and uniqueness of God. The New Testament further reveals that the one God exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The following passages provide a foundational guide for readers wishing to study the biblical basis of the doctrine of the Godhead.

The Unity of God

The foundation of biblical theology is the affirmation that there is only one true God.

Deuteronomy 6:4

"Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD."

This declaration, known as the Shema, stands at the heart of Israel's confession of faith and remains foundational to Christian belief.

Isaiah 44:6

"I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God."

Isaiah 45:5

"I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me."

Malachi 2:10

"Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?"

Mark 12:29

"The Lord our God is one Lord."

Jesus Himself affirmed the Old Testament doctrine of monotheism.

1 Timothy 2:5

"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

The New Testament never abandons belief in one God. Instead, it reveals the fullness of God's nature within that unity.

The Father is God

Scripture consistently identifies the Father as fully divine.

John 6:27

"For him hath God the Father sealed."

John 17:1–3

Jesus addresses the Father as the source of eternal life and the object of true worship.

Romans 1:7

"Grace to you and peace from God our Father."

1 Corinthians 8:6

"But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things."

Ephesians 4:6

"One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all."

1 Peter 1:2

"Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father."

The Father is presented throughout Scripture as eternal, sovereign, holy, loving, and worthy of worship.

Jesus Christ is God

One of the most important revelations of the New Testament is that Jesus Christ is fully God while remaining distinct from the Father.

John 1:1

"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

John 1:14

"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."

John 8:58

"Before Abraham was, I am."

John 10:30

"I and my Father are one."

John 20:28

"My Lord and my God."

Thomas directly acknowledges Christ's deity.

Romans 9:5

"Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever."

Philippians 2:6

"Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God."

Colossians 1:15–17

"By him were all things created."

Colossians 2:9

"For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Titus 2:13

"The great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ."

Hebrews 1:3

"The brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person."

Hebrews 1:8

"Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever."

Revelation 1:17–18

"I am the first and the last."

Titles and attributes belonging exclusively to God are repeatedly applied to Christ.

Texts Requiring Careful Reading

The doctrine of the Godhead should not be defended by collecting only those passages that appear most obviously to support it. Several texts have historically been raised as objections to the full deity of Christ or to the classical confession of the Trinity. They deserve to be read directly and in the light of the whole witness of Scripture.

John 17:3

“...thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.”

Jesus clearly distinguishes Himself from the Father to whom He prays. The verse therefore protects the personal distinction between Father and Son. It must, however, be read within the Gospel that begins by declaring “the Word was God” (John 1:1) and ends with Thomas addressing Jesus as “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). John does not resolve the distinction by denying the deity of the Son.

1 Corinthians 8:6

“But to us there is but one God, the Father... and one Lord Jesus Christ...”

Paul distinguishes Father and Son while placing both within an account of the divine source and agency of all things. The Father is the One “of whom are all things,” and Jesus Christ the One “by whom are all things.” The verse maintains monotheism without placing the Son among the things created through Him.

John 14:28

“...my Father is greater than I.”

The Son speaks within the mission in which He has taken human nature, humbled Himself and come to accomplish the Father's will. The statement expresses real relation and willing humiliation; it must be held together with the same Gospel's affirmations of His eternal pre-existence and deity.

Mark 13:32

The Son speaks of the hour as known by the Father. The text belongs to the biblical witness to Christ's genuine humanity and should not be avoided. Christian confession holds that the eternal Son truly assumed human nature rather than merely appearing to do so.

Colossians 1:15–17

Christ is called “the firstborn of every creature,” yet the passage immediately declares that all things were created by Him, that He is “before all things,” and that by Him all things consist. The surrounding verses therefore interpret “firstborn” in terms of supremacy and priority rather than placing Christ inside the created order.

Revelation 3:14

Christ is called “the beginning of the creation of God.” The statement must be read alongside Revelation's wider identification of Christ as “the first and the last” and the One who was dead and is alive for evermore. The passage cannot responsibly be isolated from the book's larger Christology.

Revelation 3:12

The risen Christ repeatedly speaks of “my God.” The language preserves the continuing distinction and relation between the Son and the Father. The exalted Christ remains the incarnate Son; His mediatorial relation does not require the conclusion that Scripture has withdrawn the divine identity it elsewhere attributes to Him.

1 Corinthians 15:24–28

Paul describes the Son delivering the kingdom to the Father and finally being subject to Him. The passage concerns the completion of Christ's mediatorial reign, when every enemy has been subdued. Personal order remains; the Son's eternal deity is not thereby revoked.

John 17:21–23

Christ prays that believers may be one as the Father and Son are one. This warns against using John 10:30 as though the word “one,” by itself, supplied a complete doctrine of the divine essence. The Trinitarian confession rests upon the cumulative biblical witness, not upon a single word detached from its contexts.

The Holy Spirit is God

The Holy Spirit is not merely a force, power, or influence. Scripture presents Him as a divine Person.

Genesis 1:2

"The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."

Psalm 139:7–8

"Whither shall I go from thy spirit?"

The Spirit possesses divine omnipresence.

Isaiah 63:10

"They rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit."

The Spirit can be grieved, demonstrating personality.

Matthew 28:19

The Holy Spirit appears alongside the Father and the Son in the baptismal formula.

John 14:16–17

Jesus speaks of the Spirit as another Comforter.

John 16:13

"He will guide you into all truth."

Acts 5:3–4

Peter identifies lying to the Holy Spirit as lying to God.

1 Corinthians 2:10–11

The Spirit possesses divine knowledge.

1 Corinthians 3:16

Believers are described as the temple of God because the Spirit dwells within them.

2 Corinthians 3:17

"Now the Lord is that Spirit."

Hebrews 9:14

The Spirit is described as eternal.

These passages establish both the personality and deity of the Holy Spirit.

The Three Persons Together

Several passages reveal the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit acting together while maintaining distinction of personhood.

Matthew 3:16–17

At Christ's baptism:

  • The Son is baptized.

  • The Spirit descends like a dove.

  • The Father's voice speaks from heaven.

This is one of the clearest Trinitarian scenes in Scripture.

Matthew 28:19

"In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."

The singular word "name" is especially significant, indicating unity alongside personal distinction.

Luke 1:35

The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are all involved in the Incarnation.

John 14:16–17

The Son asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit.

John 15:26

"The Comforter, whom I will send unto you from the Father."

Romans 15:16

Paul references the sanctifying work of the Spirit within the mission of Christ and the purpose of God.

2 Corinthians 13:14

"The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost."

This remains one of the most important Trinitarian texts in Scripture.

Ephesians 2:18

"For through him we both have access by one Spirit unto the Father."

Ephesians 4:4–6

Paul links one Spirit, one Lord, and one God and Father.

1 Peter 1:2

"Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ."

Jude 20–21

Believers pray in the Holy Spirit, remain in the love of God, and await the mercy of Jesus Christ.

Creation

Genesis 1:1–2

God creates the heaven and the earth while the Spirit of God moves upon the waters. The New Testament later reveals that all things were made through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). Read together, these passages show creation as the undivided work of the one God while revealing the Father, Son and Holy Spirit within that work.

Genesis 1:26

"Let us make man in our image."

John 1:3

"All things were made by him."

Colossians 1:16

"By him were all things created."

Psalm 104:30

"Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created."

Creation itself reflects the activity of the Godhead.

Redemption

John 3:16

The Father sends the Son.

Romans 5:8

Christ dies for sinners.

Romans 8:11

The Spirit gives life.

Galatians 4:4–6

The Father sends the Son and the Spirit.

Ephesians 1:3–14

Perhaps the clearest summary of Trinitarian salvation:

  • The Father chooses.

  • The Son redeems.

  • The Spirit seals.

Titus 3:4–6

The Father saves through the Son and renews by the Holy Spirit.

The Christian Life

Romans 8

Life in the Spirit and the believer's assurance in Christ.

Galatians 5:16–26

Walking by the Spirit and bearing His fruit.

Ephesians 4

Growing in unity, holiness, and spiritual maturity.

Philippians 2:1–11

Christ's humility as the pattern for Christian living.

1 John 4

Knowing God through love and obedient faith.

Colossians 3

Living the new life with Christ at its centre.

The Future Consummation

Acts 1:11

Christ will return.

Romans 8:19–23

Creation awaits redemption.

1 Corinthians 15:24–28

The Son's kingdom reaches its consummation.

Revelation 21:3

"The tabernacle of God is with men."

Revelation 22:1–3

The throne of God and of the Lamb stands at the centre of the new creation.

These passages illustrate the interpretive principle that governs this book. Scripture should not be protected from Scripture. A doctrine is strongest when it can receive the texts most often raised against it without suppressing them and without allowing any one of them to erase the rest of the biblical testimony. The doctrine of the Godhead rests upon that cumulative witness.

sections.title: Appendix II
sections.subtitle: Glossary of Theological Terms
sections.html:
The study of the Godhead inevitably introduces readers to theological concepts and terminology that may not be familiar to all Christians. This glossary provides concise explanations of important terms used throughout this book. While no glossary can fully capture the depth of these doctrines, the definitions below are intended to assist readers in understanding the biblical truths discussed in the preceding chapters.

Adoption

The gracious act by which God receives believers into His family and grants them the privileges and responsibilities of sons and daughters through faith in Jesus Christ.

Key Scripture: Romans 8:15–17

Advocate

A title applied to Jesus Christ, emphasizing His role as the believer's representative and intercessor before the Father.

Key Scripture: 1 John 2:1

Almighty

A title describing God's unlimited power and authority over all creation.

Key Scripture: Revelation 1:8

Ascension

The bodily return of Jesus Christ to heaven following His resurrection, where He now reigns at the Father's right hand.

Key Scripture: Acts 1:9–11

Atonement

The reconciling work accomplished by Jesus Christ through His sacrificial death on the cross, whereby sinners may be forgiven and restored to fellowship with God.

Key Scripture: Romans 5:11

Attributes of God

The qualities of God’s nature and character, such as holiness, love, justice, wisdom, omnipotence, omniscience and immutability. These belong to Him perfectly and eternally; where creatures reflect them, they do so finitely and dependently.

Key Scripture: Psalm 145:3

Baptism

The Christian ordinance symbolizing union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection and publicly identifying the believer with the Christian faith.

Key Scripture: Romans 6:3–4

Blasphemy

Speech, actions, or attitudes that dishonour, insult, or show contempt toward God.

Key Scripture: Mark 3:29

Calling

God's invitation through the Gospel whereby individuals are summoned to repentance, faith, and discipleship.

Key Scripture: Romans 8:30

Communion

Fellowship and participation in the life of God. The term is also used for the Lord's Supper.

Key Scripture: 2 Corinthians 13:14

Consummation

The final completion of God's redemptive plan at the end of history, including Christ's return, resurrection, judgment and the new creation.

Key Scripture: Revelation 21–22

Covenant

A divinely established relationship between God and humanity based upon God's promises and purposes.

Key Scripture: Genesis 17:7

Creation

The act by which God brought all things into existence from nothing through His sovereign will and power.

Key Scripture: Genesis 1:1

Deity

The divine nature or essence belonging uniquely to God.

Key Scripture: Colossians 2:9

Disciple

A follower and learner of Jesus Christ who seeks to live according to His teachings.

Key Scripture: Matthew 28:19–20

Election

God's gracious choice of individuals or a people for His redemptive purposes according to His sovereign will.

Key Scripture: Ephesians 1:4–5

Essence

A theological term used to describe what God is: the one undivided divine nature belonging equally and eternally to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Scripture does not use essence as a technical Trinitarian term; the word serves to summarise the biblical confession that there is one God while the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are each revealed as divine.

Key Scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:4; John 1:1; Matthew 28:19.

Eternal Life

The life given by God through Christ that begins at conversion and continues forever in fellowship with Him.

Key Scripture: John 17:3

Eternity

God's existence beyond the limitations of time, as well as the endless future existence of redeemed and unredeemed humanity.

Key Scripture: Psalm 90:2

Evangelism

The proclamation of the Gospel with the aim of leading people to faith in Jesus Christ.

Key Scripture: Matthew 28:19–20

Faith

Trusting reliance upon God and His promises, particularly as revealed in Jesus Christ.

Key Scripture: Hebrews 11:1

Fall

Humanity's rebellion against God through Adam and Eve, resulting in sin, death, and separation from God.

Key Scripture: Genesis 3

Foreknowledge

God's perfect and eternal knowledge of all events, persons, and realities.

Key Scripture: Romans 8:29

Glory

The majesty, splendor, beauty, and excellence of God's nature and presence.

Key Scripture: Isaiah 6:3

Godhead

A biblical English term used in the King James Version to refer to deity or the divine nature (Acts 17:29; Romans 1:20; Colossians 2:9). In this book, the Godhead is also used in the historic Christian sense as a convenient designation for the mystery of the one true God revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The doctrine of the Trinity does not arise from the word Godhead alone, but from the cumulative witness of Scripture concerning the one God and the deity and personal distinction of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Key Scriptures: Romans 1:20; Colossians 2:9; Matthew 28:19

Grace

God's undeserved favour shown toward sinners.

Key Scripture: Ephesians 2:8–9

Heaven

The realm of God’s presence and rule. Christian hope includes communion with God beyond death and culminates in bodily resurrection and life with Him in the renewed creation.

Key Scriptures: John 14:1–3; Revelation 21:1–3

Holiness

God's absolute moral perfection and separation from sin.

Key Scripture: Isaiah 6:3

Holy Spirit

The third Person of the Godhead, fully divine and eternally one with the Father and the Son.

Key Scripture: Acts 5:3–4

Hypostatic Union

The doctrine that Jesus Christ possesses two complete natures, divine and human, united in one Person without confusion or division.

Key Scripture: John 1:14

Immutability

The truth that God's nature, character and faithfulness do not change. Scripture may describe changes in God's dealings with people as circumstances change, while simultaneously affirming that He is not changeable as human beings are.

Key Scriptures: Malachi 3:6; James 1:17; 1 Samuel 15:11, 29.

Incarnation

The act whereby the eternal Son of God took upon Himself human nature and became man in the person of Jesus Christ.

Key Scripture: John 1:14

Intercession

The ministry of Christ and the Holy Spirit in pleading on behalf of believers.

Key Scripture: Romans 8:26-27, 34

Justification

God's declaration that a sinner is righteous through faith in Jesus Christ.

Key Scripture: Romans 5:1

Kingdom of God

God's sovereign rule and reign over creation, particularly as manifested through Christ.

Key Scripture: Mark 1:15

Mediator

One who stands between two parties to bring reconciliation. Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and humanity.

Key Scripture: 1 Timothy 2:5

Mercy

God's compassion toward those who deserve judgement.

Key Scripture: Titus 3:5

Omnipotence

God's unlimited power.

Key Scripture: Jeremiah 32:17

Omnipresence

God's presence everywhere at all times.

Key Scripture: Psalm 139:7–10

Omniscience

God's complete and perfect knowledge of all things.

Key Scripture: Psalm 147:5

Person

A theological term used to distinguish the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as real personal subjects who know, speak, love and relate to one another without dividing the one divine being. When used of the Godhead, Person does not mean three separate beings in the manner that three human persons are separate beings.

Key Scriptures: Matthew 3:16–17; John 14:16–17.

Predestination

God's eternal purpose concerning the destiny of His people.

Key Scripture: Romans 8:29–30

Providence

God's continuous preservation, governance and direction of creation and history through both ordinary and extraordinary means. Divine providence does not remove genuine creaturely action or make God the moral author of sin; Scripture can affirm God's sovereign purpose while holding human beings responsible for their actions.

Key Scriptures: Genesis 50:20; Daniel 4:35; Acts 2:23.

Redemption

God's act of delivering sinners from bondage to sin through Jesus Christ.

Key Scripture: Ephesians 1:7

Regeneration

The spiritual new birth accomplished by the Holy Spirit.

Key Scripture: John 3:3–8

Repentance

A turning away from sin and turning toward God.

Key Scripture: Acts 3:19

Resurrection

The raising of the dead to life. The term applies both to Christ's resurrection and to the future resurrection of humanity.

Key Scripture: 1 Corinthians 15

Revelation

God's self-disclosure to humanity through creation, Scripture, and supremely through Jesus Christ.

Key Scripture: Hebrews 1:1–2

Righteousness

Moral perfection and conformity to God's standard.

Key Scripture: Romans 3:22

Salvation

God's work of rescuing sinners from sin and reconciling them to Himself through Christ.

Key Scripture: Acts 4:12

Sanctification

The ongoing work of God whereby believers are transformed into the likeness of Christ.

Key Scripture: 1 Thessalonians 4:3

Sovereignty

God's supreme authority and rule over all creation.

Key Scripture: Psalm 103:19

Trinity

The historic Christian term for the biblical confession that there is one true God; that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are each fully divine; and that the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Holy Spirit and the Holy Spirit is not the Father. The word Trinity does not appear in Scripture. It is a theological summary intended to preserve the complete biblical witness rather than add to it.

Key Scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:4; Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14.

Worship

The response of adoration, reverence, gratitude, and obedience offered to God.

Key Scripture: John 4:23–24

Wrath

God's holy and righteous opposition to sin and evil.

Key Scripture: Romans 1:18

The terms contained in this glossary are not ends in themselves. Theology ultimately serves a higher purpose than the mastery of religious vocabulary. Its goal is the knowledge of God. As believers grow in their understanding of these truths, they are led beyond definitions and doctrines into deeper worship, stronger faith, greater obedience, and a richer appreciation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The proper end of theology is therefore not merely information but transformation. The Godhead is not simply a subject to be studied; it is the living reality at the heart of Christian faith, worship, hope, and eternal life.

sections.title: Appendix III
sections.subtitle: The Historic Creeds of the Christian Faith
sections.html:
Why Creeds Matter

The historic creeds summarise what Christians understood Scripture to teach about God, Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit, salvation and eternal life. They arose not to replace Scripture or rival its authority, but to clarify and preserve biblical truths amid competing interpretations.

This book upholds Holy Scripture as the inspired and governing authority for Christian faith and practice. The creeds are presented as historical witnesses to the Church’s efforts to confess its teachings faithfully.

The Apostles’ Creed emerged from early Christian baptismal traditions rather than direct apostolic authorship. The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed affirmed the full deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit within the one Godhead. The Athanasian Creed, despite its name, was not written by Athanasius and offers a detailed account of classical Trinitarian and Christological doctrine.

In these texts, catholic means universal, referring to the worldwide Church rather than exclusively to the Roman Catholic Church. Variations in wording across Christian traditions do not obscure their central affirmations. The Athanasian Creed’s severe declarations concerning salvation should be understood within their historical context and alongside Scripture’s wider teaching on grace, faith and judgment.

These creeds are reproduced not as inspired or exhaustive accounts of God, but as historic confessions through which readers may examine the Church’s understanding of Scripture and assess their teachings against the biblical testimony.

I. The Apostles' Creed

I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth;

And in Jesus Christ His only Son our Lord; who was conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary; suffered under Pontius Pilate; was crucified, dead and buried; He descended into hell; the third day He rose again from the dead; He ascended into heaven, and sitteth on the right hand of God the Father Almighty; from thence He shall come to judge the quick and the dead.

I believe in the Holy Ghost; the holy catholic Church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the body; and the life everlasting, Amen.

II. The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed

Commonly called the Nicene Creed

We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all worlds; God of God, Light of Light, very God of very God; begotten, not made; being of one substance with the Father; by whom all things were made;

Who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate by the Holy Ghost of the Virgin Mary, and was made Man;

And was crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate; He suffered and was buried;

And the third day He rose again according to the Scriptures;

And ascended into heaven, and sitteth on the right hand of the Father;

And He shall come again with glory to judge both the quick and the dead; whose kingdom shall have no end.

And we believe in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver of Life; who proceedeth from the Father; who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified; who spake by the prophets.

And we believe one holy catholic and apostolic Church.

We acknowledge one baptism for the remission of sins.

And we look for the resurrection of the dead,

And the life of the world to come, Amen.

III. The Athanasian Creed

Quicunque Vult

The traditional title Quicunque Vult comes from the opening Latin words, meaning “Whosoever will.” The creed’s opening and concluding clauses use severe language characteristic of the doctrinal conflicts within which it was received. They express the conviction that the identity of God and Jesus Christ is inseparable from the Gospel of salvation.

These clauses should be read within their historical and confessional setting, alongside Scripture’s complete teaching concerning salvation by grace, received through faith, and the final judgment of God. The creed is reproduced here as a historical witness to classical Christian belief, not as a replacement for Scripture or a complete statement of the Gospel.

Whosoever will be saved, before all things it is necessary that he hold the catholic faith;

Which faith except every one do keep whole and undefiled, without doubt he shall perish everlastingly.

And the catholic faith is this:

That we worship one God in Trinity, and Trinity in Unity;

Neither confounding the Persons, nor dividing the Substance.

For there is one Person of the Father, another of the Son, and another of the Holy Ghost.

But the Godhead of the Father, of the Son and of the Holy Ghost is all one: the Glory equal, the Majesty co-eternal.

Such as the Father is, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Ghost.

The Father uncreate, the Son uncreate and the Holy Ghost uncreate.

The Father incomprehensible, the Son incomprehensible and the Holy Ghost incomprehensible.

The Father eternal, the Son eternal and the Holy Ghost eternal.

And yet they are not three eternals, but one Eternal.

As also there are not three incomprehensibles, nor three uncreated, but one Uncreated and one Incomprehensible.

So likewise the Father is Almighty, the Son Almighty and the Holy Ghost Almighty.

And yet they are not three Almighties, but one Almighty.

So the Father is God, the Son is God and the Holy Ghost is God.

And yet they are not three Gods, but one God.

So likewise the Father is Lord, the Son Lord and the Holy Ghost Lord.

And yet not three Lords, but one Lord.

For like as we are compelled by the Christian verity to acknowledge every Person by Himself to be both God and Lord;

So are we forbidden by the catholic religion to say: There be three Gods, or three Lords.

The Father is made of none; neither created nor begotten.

The Son is of the Father alone; not made nor created, but begotten.

The Holy Ghost is of the Father and of the Son; neither made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.

So there is one Father, not three Fathers; one Son, not three Sons; one Holy Ghost, not three Holy Ghosts.

And in this Trinity none is before or after another; none is greater or less than another.

But the whole three Persons are co-eternal together and co-equal.

So that in all things, as aforesaid, the Unity in Trinity and the Trinity in Unity is to be worshipped.

He therefore that will be saved must thus think of the Trinity.

Furthermore, it is necessary to everlasting salvation that he also believe rightly the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For the right faith is that we believe and confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is God and Man;

God, of the Substance of the Father, begotten before the worlds; and Man, of the substance of His mother, born in the world;

Perfect God and perfect Man, of a reasonable soul and human flesh subsisting;

Equal to the Father, as touching His Godhead; and inferior to the Father, as touching His Manhood.

Who, although He be God and Man, yet He is not two, but one Christ;

One, not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh, but by taking of the Manhood into God;

One altogether, not by confusion of Substance, but by unity of Person.

For as the reasonable soul and flesh is one man, so God and Man is one Christ;

Who suffered for our salvation, descended into hell, rose again the third day from the dead;

He ascended into heaven, He sitteth on the right hand of the Father, God Almighty, from whence He shall come to judge the quick and the dead.

At whose coming all men shall rise again with their bodies;

And shall give account for their own works.

And they that have done good shall go into life everlasting; and they that have done evil into everlasting fire.

This is the catholic faith, which except a man believe faithfully, he cannot be saved, Amen.

sections.title: Appendix V
sections.subtitle: Questions for Personal Reflection and Group Discussion
sections.html:
The following questions are intended to help readers engage more personally and thoughtfully with the principal themes of this book. They are not designed merely to test recollection, but to encourage honest reflection, meaningful conversation and a deeper consideration of the God revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

The first section may be used privately after completing the book. The second is designed for church groups, study circles, families and other settings in which readers can examine the book’s arguments together.

Personal Reflection

  1. Before reading this book, what place did the knowledge of God occupy in your understanding of yourself, the world and the purpose of life?

  2. What experiences, relationships or inherited convictions have most strongly shaped the way you think about God?

  3. Are there truths about God that you formally believe but do not yet consistently use to interpret your circumstances, ambitions or decisions?

  4. How has the distinction between knowing about God and knowing God affected the way you understand your own faith?

  5. Which aspect of the biblical revelation of the Father, the Son or the Holy Spirit became clearer or more personally significant to you while reading this book?

  6. Which objection considered in Chapter Six did you find most challenging, and how adequately did the chapter address it?

  7. In what area of your life is there presently the greatest distance between what you confess about God and the way you habitually think, choose or respond?

  8. How should knowing the Triune God reshape your approach to work, family, ambition, suffering, prayer and service?

  9. What legitimate pursuit or responsibility may have begun to carry a weight of identity or ultimate meaning that it was never intended to bear?

  10. Having completed the book, how would you now answer its opening question—Who is God?—and what practical difference should that answer make to the way you live?

Group Discussion

  1. Can human beings acquire genuine knowledge, exercise moral judgment and accomplish worthwhile things without consciously acknowledging God? What, according to this book, remains incomplete in such knowledge?

  2. Why must knowledge of God begin with divine self-revelation rather than human imagination, philosophical speculation or religious preference?

  3. How would the group explain the Christian confession of one God in three Persons without suggesting either three gods or one Person appearing in three temporary roles?

  4. Why does the doctrine of the Godhead rest upon the cumulative witness of Scripture rather than upon the word Trinity or any single biblical passage?

  5. Which objection presented in Chapter Six is most likely to trouble readers from Christian, secular, Jewish or Muslim backgrounds? How should Christians respond with both conviction and respect?

  6. How can divine sovereignty and genuine human responsibility be affirmed together without making God the author of evil or reducing human choices to an illusion?

  7. In what ways should the Church’s worship, fellowship, exercise of spiritual gifts and public witness reveal the character and work of the Triune God?

  8. What is the difference between biblical hope and either withdrawal from the world or excessive speculation about future events?

  9. Where does contemporary civilisation most clearly demonstrate the difference between increasing human capability and increasing wisdom, particularly in relation to artificial intelligence, government, commerce or law?

  10. If the knowledge of God is truly the foundation of everything else, what should change in the way Christians participate in family life, professional work, leadership, public affairs and service to their communities?

CONCLUDING REFLECTION

These questions are intended to do more than complete an intellectual exercise. They invite readers to consider whether truth received by the mind has begun to illuminate the life.

The knowledge of God reaches its proper end when it leads us to worship Him more faithfully, trust Him more completely and walk with Him more consciously.
